title: Apple has big October coming for new hardware and software, here’s the lineup
snippet: Apple has a big October ahead, with several major hardware and software launches coming. Here’s everything to expect from Apple in October. more…
fullText:
Apple has a big October ahead, with several major hardware and software launches coming. Here’s everything to expect from Apple in October.

iPhone Duo launches October 23

iPhone Duo is confirmed to arrive in users’ hands in October. Pre-orders open Friday, October 16 and the first units deliver on October 23.

Apple’s first foldable model might be limited in supply. However, iPhone Duo is launching in lots of countries simultaneously, which could be a good sign for availability. Per Apple:

Customers in more than 70 countries and regions, including Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, France, Germany, India, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, Singapore, South Korea, Türkiye, the UAE, the UK, the U.S., and Vietnam, will be able to pre-order iPhone Duo beginning at 5 a.m. PT on Friday, October 16, with availability beginning Friday, October 23. iPhone Duo will be available in 28 other countries and regions beginning Friday, October 30.

If iPhone Duo supply was expected to be significantly lower than anticipated demand, it’s unlikely Apple would launch the product in close to 100 countries and regions right away.

Read more: Apple unveils foldable iPhone Duo

Hardware rumors: New Macs, Home products, and iPad mini

Apple reportedly has a lot more new hardware products launching in October too. We’re expecting new Macs, Home products, and an upgraded iPad mini. Here’s what’s rumored:

Touchscreen MacBook Pro / Ultra: All-new design for high-end MacBook with OLED, more

M6 iMac: Powerful chip and new color options

M6 MacBook Pro: Update for 14-inch base MacBook Pro

New Apple TV 4K: A19 or A19 Pro chip, Siri AI, new Siri Remote

HomePad: New home hub with built-in touchscreen

HomePod mini 2: More powerful chip, audio upgrades, more

iPad mini: OLED display, A19 Pro or A20 Pro chip

Two standout products include the first touchscreen Mac, which could be branded MacBook Pro or Ultra, and the long-expected home hub ‘HomePad.’ Everything else will be smaller updates to existing products.

Software launches: iOS 27.1 and iOS 27.2, more

Apple has confirmed that iPhone Duo will run on iOS 27.1 when it launches in October. 

It’s speculated that 27.1 will be Duo-exclusive. However, it might come to other iPhones too, but only include bug fixes or security updates while the majority of changes are for Apple’s foldable.

Normally we would expect more features in iOS 27.1, but in an unusual move, iOS 27.2 is already in testing and is also expected to arrive in October. As a result, iOS 27.2 is likely intended for all iPhones while 27.1 is primarily for iPhone Duo. 

New features in iOS 27.2 so far include:

Profiles for the Apple TV app come to iPhone and iPad

Dual Capture feature available for Group FaceTime calls

Siri AI expands to several new languages

New features for Apple Music, CarPlay Ultra, and more might be coming too

When iOS 27 launched, Apple confirmed that Siri AI “will expand to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish next month.“ Since that language expansion is included in iOS 27.2, we’re expecting both 27.1 and 27.2 to arrive before October ends.

The iOS 27.2 beta also includes an all-new Health app with Apple Intelligence features, but it’s expected to be removed from the shipping version and return in iOS 27.3 later this year instead.

Read more: Here’s everything new Apple TV has coming in October

Which new hardware and software launches in October are you most excited for? Let us know in the comments.

title: Apple faces class action over Apple Pay fees charged to card issuers
snippet: U.S. District Judge Jeffrey S. White has certified a class-action lawsuit accusing Apple of charging payment card issuers inflated fees for Apple Pay transactions. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
U.S. District Judge Jeffrey S. White has certified a class-action lawsuit accusing Apple of charging payment card issuers inflated fees for Apple Pay transactions. Here are the details.

As first spotted by AppleInsider, a federal judge has allowed an antitrust lawsuit over Apple Pay fees to proceed as a class action, meaning payment card issuers across the U.S. may now pursue their claims against Apple as a group.

In a press release from Hagens Berman, the law firm representing the plaintiffs, the firm said the certified class includes all U.S. entities that issued payment cards enabled for Apple Pay and paid Apple fees on transactions made with those cards.

The firm argues that while mobile wallets on Android do not charge card issuers transaction fees, Apple charges U.S. issuers 0.15% on credit card transactions and 0.5 cents on debit card transactions made through Apple Pay.

From the press release:

The lawsuit accuses Apple of extracting up to $1 billion annually in fees in violation of federal antitrust law. Apple denies rivals access to the technology needed to develop a competing mobile wallet, according to the class action. On iOS devices, Apple has ensured that only its mobile wallet, Apple Pay, can make contactless payments at the point of sale. Having secured a monopoly for Apple Pay in this fashion, Apple charges card issuers who use Apple Pay, like credit unions and other small financial institutions, supracompetitive fees for a service that is available on Android devices for free, according to the lawsuit.

The firm also highlighted that Judge White “denied Apple’s motion to exclude expert testimony attorneys say establishes common proof that Apple maintains monopoly power in a relevant antitrust aftermarket for tap-and-pay iOS mobile wallets as well as a broader market for all mobile wallets.”

The lawsuit seeks reimbursement for card issuers that paid Apple Pay fees, as well as an injunction against Apple’s challenged policies.

title: Apple has three products launching soon that we’ve waited a long time for
snippet: Apple had a big September, but it’s set to keep momentum going in October with several rumored product unveilings soon that we’ve waited a long time for. more…
fullText:
Apple had a big September, but it’s set to keep momentum going in October with several rumored product unveilings soon that we’ve waited a long time for.

#1: MacBook Pro / Ultra redesign with touchscreen

The Mac is a long-time touchscreen holdout, but that’s finally set to change with a new MacBook Pro (or MacBook Ultra) product expected to launch in October.

Apple’s next-gen MacBook Pro will introduce a brand new industrial design—the first such overhaul in five years. And in addition to touch support, it will boast an OLED display, Dynamic Island, and possibly a C2 cellular modem option.

It’s been a long time since the MacBook Pro got a new look. But far longer since touchscreens became the norm, and Apple decided to forego them on the Mac. I’m excited to see how touch might enhance the experience of the Mac moving forward.

#2: New Apple TV 4K

There’s never been a longer wait for new Apple TV hardware than the current drought of updates. Apple’s latest model, the third-gen Apple TV 4K, was introduced in 2022.

Rumors indicate we’ll finally get a new Apple TV 4K in October, headlined by a powerful A19 or A19 Pro chip and Siri AI support.

This summer Apple raised prices on most of its products, including the Apple TV. That means the four-year-old Apple TV 4K now costs $199—far more than the $129 price it launched at. Here’s hoping the new Apple TV doesn’t go any higher.

#3: ‘HomePad’

Rumors of a HomePod with a display have been around for nearly as long as the HomePod’s existence. But they ramped up in 2024 when Mark Gurman offered an in-depth report on what’s commonly called the ‘HomePad.’

	

HomePad is a smart display with built-in speaker that will reportedly spearhead Apple’s renewed push into home products. It will have a new OS that resembles parts of iOS, tvOS, and watchOS, including a StandBy-like mode.

Siri AI is expected to be central to the product, which will also feature a camera, customizable widgets, and built-in Apple apps like Photos, Notes, Music, Calendar, and more.

title: Motorola Signature 27 confirmed to support GrapheneOS
snippet: It’s confirmed: The mysterious Motorola phone getting support for the privacy-focused GrapheneOS will be the Motorola Signature 27 that was announced earlier this week. more…
fullText:
It’s confirmed: The mysterious Motorola phone getting support for the privacy-focused GrapheneOS will be the Motorola Signature 27 that was announced earlier this week.

GrapheneOS, a privacy-focused take on Android that’s grown popular in recent years, has so far only been available on Pixel devices. That’s for a number of reasons relating back to how Google handles the software and the security components in Pixel (and Tensor) hardware.

But, now, GrapheneOS is officially stepping beyond Pixel and into a device that will come pre-loaded with its version of Android. It was announced that this would be a Motorola device, but which device was left a mystery as all existing Motorola devices were not compatible with the platform.

Unsurprisingly, though, the first GrapheneOS device from Motorola will be the Motorola Signature 27. GrapheneOS confirmed the news on Twitter/X, though other details are still minimal. It’s apparently still planned that devices will be sold with GrapheneOS pre-installed. The Signature 27 was announced earlier this week and its use of the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset is likely a major part of the reason it will be able to run GrapheneOS properly.

	

An exact release date for the Motorola Signature 27 has yet to be confirmed, and it’s unclear if GrapheneOS will be available right away either. It’s already known that future versions of Razr flip and Razr Fold will also support the privacy-focused OS.

title: Opera’s free built-in VPN can now turn on automatically when using public Wi-Fi
snippet: Opera announced today that its free, built-in VPN for desktop can now automatically activate when users connect to public or unsecured Wi-Fi networks. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Opera announced today that its free, built-in VPN for desktop can now automatically activate when users connect to public or unsecured Wi-Fi networks. Here are the details.

Opt-in feature rolls out today in the US and France

Since 2016, the Opera browser has offered a free, built-in VPN. The company says this builds on its core belief that “making basic online privacy accessible to everyone.”

In recent years, VPNs have gone from being a relatively niche privacy tool to something much more mainstream. Still, according to data from We Are Social’s Digital 2026 Mid-Year Global Update Report, only 23% of internet users aged 16 and older use a VPN for at least some of their online activities.

That is a problem, particularly for users who rely on public Wi-Fi for work or while traveling.

Today, Opera announced that users in the US and France can opt to have its built-in VPN turn on automatically whenever they connect to a public or unsecured Wi-Fi network.

Here’s Opera:

Public Wi-Fi networks are notoriously vulnerable to snooping and data interception. Opera’s browser VPN now removes manual friction by automatically activating when detecting public or unsecured Wi-Fi networks. Users can study, work, manage finances, or browse without having to remember to turn on protection manually. To respect user agency, the feature remains strictly opt-in and can be easily toggled within settings. This functionality is rolling out today to Opera users in the US and France.

Opera notes that its “free VPN operates under strict GDPR laws,” adding that it “has been independently audited by Deloitte.” The company also stresses that the VPN is part of a broader set of built-in privacy tools, alongside Opera’s native Ad Blocker and Tracker Blocker.

title: New iPad mini coming soon with these major changes
snippet: Apple is about to release a new iPad mini. This will mark the first update to the device in two years, and it’s expected to be a big one. Here’s everything we know so far about the new iPad mini coming as soon as next month. more…
fullText:
Apple is about to release a new iPad mini. This will mark the first update to the device in two years, and it’s expected to be a big one. Here’s everything we know so far about the new iPad mini coming as soon as next month.

OLED display

By far the biggest change to the new iPad mini will be to the display. According to multiple sources, the iPad mini 8 will feature an OLED display.

This will be a dramatic improvement to the iPad mini’s current LCD panel. For users, the move to OLED means deeper blacks, richer colors, and better contrast. The iPhone X was the first iPhone to use an OLED display in 2017, while the OLED iPad Pro debuted in 2024.

One lingering question, though, is whether the new iPad mini will use a ProMotion display for refresh rates of up to 120Hz. According to a sketchy rumor last week, the new iPad mini won’t offer ProMotion support and will instead be limited to 60Hz.

This hasn’t been corroborated by any other sources, though, so I’m holding out hope this leak is incorrect.

New chip

The current iPad mini, released in October 2024, is powered by Apple’s A17 Pro chip. The new iPad mini will likely feature the A19 Pro or A20 Pro chip. This will offer a solid boost in performance, and could enable support for the most advanced Siri AI features in iOS 27.

Better water resistance

According to Bloomberg, Apple has tested a “redesigned casing” for the iPad mini that is water-resistant like the iPhone.

Whether or not this water-resistant casing pans out remains to be seen. However, it would make the iPad mini far more durable. It’d be especially notable for people who use it as an e-reader, as one of the top features of dedicated e-readers like the Kindle is water resistance.

New speaker technology

The iPad mini 8 might also be Apple’s first device with a revamped vibration-based speaker system. This vibration-based speaker system would let Apple remove speaker holes, aiding its work to make the device water-resistant.

In contrast, the iPhone has speaker holes, but Apple uses gaskets and adhesives to make the device water-resistant.

New iPad mini release date

According to the latest reporting from Bloomberg, Apple is aiming to release the OLED iPad mini as early as this October. It’s allegedly the “biggest overhaul to the iPad mini in half a decade.”

There’s no word on how much the new iPad mini will cost. Apple increased the price of the current iPad mini in July from $499 to $599 (currently discounted to $569 on Amazon). Whether the new iPad mini with OLED is even more expensive remains to be seen.

What do you think of Apple’s rumored plans for the iPad mini? Are you tempted by the OLED display? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Google rolling out blood pressure & insulin resistance, more on Pixel Watch 3, 4, 5
snippet: As previewed during last month’s Pixel Watch 5 launch, Google is now starting to roll out blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality metrics. more…
fullText:
As previewed during last month’s Pixel Watch 5 launch, Google is now starting to roll out blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality metrics.

Health Guardian is Google’s overarching brand for the Pixel Watch’s suite of “proactive health and safety tools.” It includes Breathing Emergency Detection, which is available in Europe on the Pixel Watch 4 and 5.

The blood pressure trends feature works by passively measuring your pulse and motion patterns over the course of a month. It’s intended to let you detect “persistent higher cardiovascular trends early.” This works without a cuff or manual calibration, and was trained using billions of minutes of raw heart and movement data. You need “at least 5 consecutive days in a week” of data.

Insulin resistance trends analyze multi-week physiological data to track shifts in metabolic health without requiring a blood draw. Insulin resistance impacts how your body absorbs energy from food, with Google needing a minimum of 7 days of data in a month. The feature uses Google’s largest sensor foundational model. It was pre-trained using over 1 trillion minutes of data from 5 million opted-in users.

	
	

Both sets of trend insights will appear in the Google Health app on the first day of each month.

Meanwhile, sleep breathing quality metrics will track overnight breathing changes. In the morning, you’ll see how much time was spent optimally breathing, while a monthly report identifies longer-term patterns.

Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5 users will be able to set up these three features in the Google Health app starting this week. Access is free on those three devices, with the first trend reports coming in early October.

If you’re a Google Health Premium subscriber, these three features are also coming to the Fitbit Air “later this year.”

title: I created an interactive digital avatar of myself — and you can talk to it
snippet: After obtaining an interactive avatar and training it to discuss venture fraud, I have mixed feelings about making AI clones of ourselves.
fullText:
When Alexandru Voica, head of corporate affairs at the video-generation startup Synthesia, sent me a link this summer to the newest addition to their PR team, I was surprised. It was an interactive virtual avatar of him, trained to answer common press questions about Synthesia, like what it does and how it works. The day before, I was on a panel where PR people asked me if I minded pitches that used AI-generated text. But Alexandru’s avatar was beyond that — this seemed to me the final boss of using AI in PR. 

In September, Synthesia invited me to its new office space in New York. Originally based in the U.K., Synthesia is a hot digital avatar startup alongside others like D-ID, HeyGen, and Colossyan. It hit a $4 billion valuation earlier this year and said last year it had crossed $100 million in ARR.

Synthesia lets enterprises build interactive training videos with AI avatars and recently launched a product called Roleplay Sessions that lets employees practice, for example, sales pitches with an interactive AI avatar that responds and scores their responses.

When I went to the new office opening and they asked me if I would like my own AI avatar, I didn’t even hesitate to say yes. Of course I would like my own digital twin. My outfit was cute that day, and my hair was in place.

Until I met my digital twin, I had been indifferent toward avatars, but I felt they would inevitably become part of everyday online life. I heard of people on Instagram creating them in their likenesses to help them make social content. I find it all to be very interesting, and it’s perhaps why I have no qualms now presenting to you my digital twin. This is the first time Synethsia has made a digital avatar for a journalist (or for anyone, period, outside of Voica). It is trained on my story about why venture-backed startups commit more fraud than non-VC-backed startups and will only answer questions about that story. 

Below, simply press “start in a new window” to begin.

You can ask it questions like:

Why did I decide to write this story?

What is the research paper about?

What did the researchers find?

To make this, I entered a mini film studio nestled inside Synthesia’s office where they took numerous photos of me and captured a two-minute recording of my voice. I had to consent to these avatars being made and, well, digital Dom was born. They created a personal avatar for me (one that just reads whatever script I give it) — with and without glasses — and they made two interactive avatars for me (ones that can talk back and listen to me), also with and without glasses. 

We picked an article to train the interactive avatar on, and then one of the teams built my interactive avatar, which is powered by a combination of voice-to-text, video, language, and text-to-voice models. My avatar’s tech stack includes Synthesia’s own video and voice models, although the company also allows customers to choose alternatives from other labs like Cartesia, ElevenLabs, Google, or OpenAI. Enterprises can also choose to host their avatars on whatever cloud they want or pay Synthesia to host them.

The voice-to-text model turns what people say into text, the agentic language model makes sense of text and can take actions based on it, the text-to-voice model turns a response into audio, and finally a video model (built by Synthesia) animates the avatar as it talks. 

Overall, Synthesia builds three types of products — a video-creation and distribution platform with classic avatars, where someone types in a script and the avatar repeats it; an agentic platform called Sessions where people can interact with the avatars in surveys or roleplay; and an API platform where people can take Synthesia video and voice models and combine them with other tech services to build interactive avatars or other types of products.

It took the Synthesia team a couple of days to make my avatars. I played first with the personal ones and typed a fairly generic script to see how my AI voice sounded. I had it talk about how fall has arrived in New York, my favorite time of year. The voice was fairly accurate, and I was glad it didn’t pick up any of the hoarseness I had when I recorded my audio sample. 

I showed it to some non-tech friends who found it both interesting and creepy.

Then I showed them my interactive one, which is deterministic, meaning it will only say what it was trained to respond to. In this case, that was my venture fraud story. I asked it questions like where I was before TechCrunch and what part of New York I lived in, but each time it directed me back to the story. 

My friends didn’t think the voice sounded much like mine and thought the likeness was not as good as the personal avatar, but nonetheless it was close enough to be somewhat creepy. My mom called it “amazing,” which is pretty high praise from her. She and my father kept trying to ask it questions “only they would know” about me — but the model didn’t answer, redirecting them each time to the venture fraud story. 

“I don’t remember giving birth to two of you,” she joked after testing the model.

This experience has made me think about what the future of journalism could be. Would people be OK with turning on the news and it being presented by an avatar? One investor told me no immediately. Certainly there is a lot of pushback today on AI slop that has infiltrated social media and other news-sharing platforms. But others I asked weren’t so sure. Could avatars augment — or even replace — journalists? Would CEOs want to talk to an AI avatar of a journalist rather than a human one? 

What I like about my career is connecting with people, writing stories, and researching new topics. But the biggest part of journalism is trust. That doesn’t seem like it could ever be outsourced to an AI. 

Outside of journalism, I’m confident the idea of cloning yourself could be appealing. No more catching up on work after a holiday or vacation, because a version of you can always be around, answering questions.

We’ll have to see how avatar usage evolves in corporate America. But now that I have my own, I have mixed feelings. After I got over the initial novelty of it, I examined my avatar closely after it stopped talking and waited — for what, I’m not sure. Maybe I’m waiting for it to blink. Or to say something new, or to smile, or to just let me know that it knows. 

Because my digital twins are deterministic, they will never do that. But I can see how easy it would be for someone to fall into a tinge of AI psychosis with one that was nondeterministic, meaning powered by a chatbot that was free to pontificate.

I told one investor that, whatever the future of digital twins is, I predict that my generation, Gen Z, likely won’t get used to them. They feel sci-fi: Everything we’ve ever seen in a movie is here now. But I will say, I find digital avatars less jarring than humanoids. At least with an avatar, if stuff gets weird, I can always log off. 

Until then, however, here is my personal avatar, giving you a rundown of all the top stories on our site this week!

When Alexandru Voica, head of corporate affairs at the video-generation startup Synthesia, sent me a link this summer to the newest addition to their PR team, I was surprised. It was an interactive virtual avatar of him, trained to answer common press questions about Synthesia, like what it does and how it works. The day before, I was on a panel where PR people asked me if I minded pitches that used AI-generated text. But Alexandru’s avatar was beyond that — this seemed to me the final boss of using AI in PR.

title: Apple Card adds new feature in iOS 27 that every card should have
snippet: iOS 27 brings a variety of new features to Apple Wallet, including one exclusive to Apple Card that I wish every card offered: a hub for all recurring transactions. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brings a variety of new features to Apple Wallet, including one exclusive to Apple Card that I wish every card offered: a hub for all recurring transactions.

iOS 27 shows Apple Card recurring transactions in one place, making it easy to track subscriptions

Subscriptions are increasingly popular in the digital-centric world. As such, it can be easy to lose track of everything you’re subscribed to.

While plenty of apps and services offer to keep track of your subscriptions, giving third parties access to your financial info can spark privacy concerns. Fortunately, those solutions soon won’t be needed for Apple Card.

In iOS 27, the Wallet app offers a new feature for Apple Card users: a recurring transaction section.

When viewing your Apple Card in iOS 27, there’s a new ‘Recurring’ option inside the three-dot menu in the top-right corner.

Tapping this will show you a list of upcoming recurring transactions, and even lets you see them on a monthly calendar view.

I like to think I have a pretty good sense of all the things I’m subscribed to. But that takes effort. And Apple Card’s new feature makes tracking subscriptions pretty effortless.

I’m especially a fan of the calendar view, as it’s so nice getting to see at a glance exactly when each charge is expected to go through.

iOS 27 lists recurring transactions based on your Apple Card history, so it won’t always catch everything. The Wallet app has a disclaimer that states: “Dates and amounts shown are predicted based on your transaction history and may not be exact. Routine spending may incorrectly appear as recurring.”

If you do see an item that’s incorrectly marked as recurring, it’s easy to correct the error.

I really hope Apple Card inspires more credit cards and banks to copy iOS 27’s new feature. It feels like a no-brainer addition that every card should have.

Now I want to start moving all my subscriptions on to Apple Card.

snippet: After a slight delay, Samsung is rolling out its Android 17-based One UI 9 update to Galaxy S26 owners in the US, though not to everyone just yet. more…
fullText:
After a slight delay, Samsung is rolling out its Android 17-based One UI 9 update to Galaxy S26 owners in the US, though not to everyone just yet.

Samsung announced the rollout of One UI 9 as starting earlier this month, but the update failed to show up and, in some regions, Samsung even briefly confirmed a delay. While the exact speed bumps Samsung hit are unclear, the rollout appears to be commencing.

On Reddit, a handful of Galaxy S26 series owners in the US confirmed that One UI 9 has reached their devices. The roughly 4GB update is showing up for users on T-Mobile, but carrier rollouts are typically a sign that more devices are set to join the rollout soon. Oddly, unlocked devices do not appear to be getting the update just yet.

title: Motorola Signature 27 is a proper flagship with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Alongside Qualcomm’s latest announcements, Motorola has officially shown off the Motorola Signature 27, a true flagship offering that’s set to launch before the end of this year. more…
fullText:
Alongside Qualcomm’s latest announcements, Motorola has officially shown off the Motorola Signature 27, a true flagship offering that’s set to launch before the end of this year.

Building on the Motorola Signature, a pseudo-flagship that launched earlier this year, the Signature 27 adopts a new naming scheme (based on the coming year), a wild-looking design, and a proper flagship spec sheet.

While its predecessor was based on Qualcomm’s step-down Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, the Motorola Signature 27 uses the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, a new chip that’s just as powerful as its mouthful of a name. It’s a big deal on Motorola’s part, as the brand hasn’t used any flagship chipsets in quite a while. The Motorola Razr Ultra (2025) used the Snapdragon 8 Elite, but its successor didn’t upgrade, and other devices in the company’s lineup, including the $1,900 Razr Fold, haven’t gone beyond the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5.

Qualcomm announces the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

Motorola says to expect stronger on-device AI features with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, as well as “responsive” gaming, faster download speeds over various networks, and improvements to the camera, too. There’s an “ArcticMesh” cooling system that combines a 40% larger vapor chamber with liquid metal, copper mesh, and “diamond-infused thermal gel.”

	

Motorola Signature 27 is promised 7 years of Android OS and security updates and has quite the look with its quad-camera setup on the back. That includes a 50MP Sony LYTIA 910 main sensor and 200MP periscope telephoto lens. The other two haven’t been confirmed just yet. The design itself brings back some Droid Razr vibes from over a decade ago. 

Signature 27 will come in “Coal Smoke” with a “Tactical Weave” finish, or “Capulet Green” with a “brushed textile-inspired finish.”

A firm release date hasn’t been announced, nor has Motorola spilled the beans on exact launch markets. The company says it will debut “worldwide” in 2026, and also confirmed a launch in North America in the “coming months.”

Right before all of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo craziness, I was lucky enough to attend my first IFA in Berlin. For those unaware, IFA is the CES of Europe. There are thousands of brands and companies, ranging from tiny start-ups to giant juggernauts. They all have one goal: to show off what they have been creating to the 100,000s of visitors that attend. 

I saw everything from flying cars to mini robots to 200-inch transparent displays, and while all of those products are awesome for a quick demo and to show off, I was not there for them. I wanted to see the tech that is actually about to come out, not the tech that maybe one day will see the light of day. So here are my favorite products from IFA, with a bit of an Apple twist, of course!

Lexar Muse

I have been, and still am, a huge Lexar SSD user. They make reliable, fast, and compact SSDs that I use in my workflow daily. I currently use their SL500 and their magnetic SSD with my iPhone 18 Pro Max. They are versatile and work in my Apple ecosystem because they have the speed to support that ProRes Raw footage. But their newest announcement, the Lexar Muse, blew me away. I am a huge fan of thin tech, so when I saw that this SSD is just 3.8mm at its thickest point, I was all over this. 

Just 3.8mm at its thickest point, tapering to 1mm at the edges

Up to 1,050 MB/s read and 1,000 MB/s write

512GB and 1TB

Proprietary PogoPin connection with a SnapLink Magnetic Cable

Supports direct external Apple ProRes 4K recording at up to 120 fps on compatible iPhones

The main thing I was curious about was how you can fit a USB-C port on such a small device. The answer is: you can’t. So what they created was a pogo pin connection. You just slap the SSD to the rear of your iPhone with the Magsafe accessory, and it comes with a USB-C to pogo pin cable. It’s sized perfectly to be long enough to not be in the way and reach the back of the Lexar Muse. I thought this was a genius use case. 

As of now, given how thin it is and the current storage crisis, Lexar will be offering these in 512 MB and 1 TB sizes, with higher capacities in the future. It is set to release in October of 2026!

Belkin LilyPad

Now this one is more of a guilty pleasure than anything else. I recently took my 5-year-old to her first movie theater experience, and we went to see the new Toy Story 5. If you have yet to see it, the main villain in the movie is an iPad-like tablet called LilyPad that eventually turns good and becomes an ally of all the main characters. So when I saw the actual LilyPad character at the Belkin booth, I had to stop by. Turns out that this is part of a much bigger collaboration that brings all the characters to a bunch of Apple-friendly accessories. But the show stopper here is the LilyPad case because it turns your iPad into that character. 

Officially licensed Disney Pixar Toy Story 5 Lilypad character design

Compatbile with iPad 10th generation (10.9-inch) and iPad 11th generation (11-inch A16)

Shock-absorbing EVA foam construction with rounded edges and 4-foot drop protection

Integrated handle with an easy-grip texture designed for smaller hands

Built-in kickstand

Exclusive and licensed Lilypad wallpapers included

But as I mentioned, this is an entire collection. Belkin has also made a Toy Story iPhone case, a MagSafe power bank, and a larger power bank that resembles one of the toys from the movie. I think these were tastefully done, as they still provide plenty of functionality and look fun for any Toy Story fan. All of these products are available today and range from $35 to $55, with the LilyPad being $49. 

Wokyis i5 Docking Station

I am a huge fan of Wokyis products. They have found a way to bring a nostalgic look and feel to products that bring modern functionality. I recently reviewed their G5 and G7 docks for the Mac mini and the Mac Studio. But those are built to physically be attached to the Mac. So what Wokyis did was bring all that function and nostalgia to a standalone dock that works with any computer. You get all the pro-level ports you needed and a display as well!

Built-in 5-inch HD IPS display with a 1280 × 720 resolution

Four dedicated shortcut keys and a rotary control knob for frequently used functions

Built-in M.2 NVMe SSD enclosure for additional storage

Four USB-A ports, one USB-C data port, SD and microSD 4.0 card readers, HDMI input, and a 3.5mm headphone jack with up to 10Gbps speeds

Supports up to 65W pass-through charging for compatible laptops

As I mentioned, I love products with a bit of character. I want my accessories to be conversation starters, making people wonder and say, “What is that?” That is exactly what Wokyis products do, and the i5 Docking Station is no different. It brings some awesome personality at a time when most docks are completely sterile. 

The i5 Docking Station is available on Amazon today for $153. If you need a new docking station that adds a bit of fun and tactility without sacrificing function, this is a good one to grab.

iPhone cases 

You can just imagine the thousands, if not millions, of different iPhone case brands that were at IFA. From every shape, material, size, and function, there is a case for any type of person. The thing about cases is that they are completely subjective. There is no real good or bad, or right or wrong. You either like it or you don’t. But there are two cases I wanted to highlight because they are different from some of the others I have seen. 

First is the Xtrem Inno cases. I reviewed their first gen last year and loved it because I had never seen another case do this. The Xtrem Inno case has a Color E ink display that allows you to change what it shows on the rear of the case to anything you want. 

Circular, customizable rear display with four-color reproduction and a resolution of 212 PPI

The display requires no separate charging and retains its image without continuously consuming power

Supports MagSafe wireless charging and magnetic accessories

On the surface, it looks like a nicely designed case, but when you pair it with their app, you can send an image via NFC to the case. It’s so cool how it all works. The amazing thing is that since it uses NFC and E-ink, that means no batteries, Bluetooth, or wired connections are needed. The phone uses a tiny bit of power to send the image via NFC, and since it’s E-ink, once it’s on, it stays on without persistent power.

The case is available today on Amazon for $75 and comes in a ton of new colors. If you need a fun new case, this is the way to go. 

Moft Movas Coffee Edition

Last year, Moft introduced a new ultra-thin case for the iPhone 17 lineup. The base itself was great for anyone who wanted a super-slim, minimal case. They ended up bringing it back for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, but the interesting part is the material they went with, more than anything else. At a time when sustainability is high on the agenda, Moft decided to use a new coffee-based bio-leather for this case, and it’s awesome. The best part is that it gives off a bit of a coffee aroma. So this is the case for all my coffee lovers out there! Outside of that, you get all the trimmings you want out of a rthin case.

Built-in magnets for MagSafe

Weighs just 28g and is ultra-thin

Reinforced TPU corners provide basic drop protection, while the open-sided frame design preserves the natural feel of the iPhone

Available in a Coffee Brown and Sapphire Blue color combination

Again, the innovation here is the choice of material. I had never heard of or seen this choice of using coffee grounds to create a sort of bio-leather. They are also using this material for their famous moft wallet stand. They are all available on Amazon today for $49. 

Final thoughts

Again, there was a ton, and I mean a ton of things that came from IFA that I am excited about. I was able to see things like ultra-fast supercars, the Xiaomi iPhone Duo clone before it was announced, and so much more. But these were just a few of the things that caught my eye and made sense to me in our Apple-focused world. 

Did you happen to catch any of the IFA excitement? What were some of the products that caught your eye?

title: MacWhisper update brings real-time meeting transcripts, improved speaker recognition, more
snippet: My transcription tool of choice on the Mac, MacWhisper, got another major update today with real-time meeting transcripts, significantly improved speaker recognition, tighter integration with Apple Intelligence, and a new transcription model. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
My transcription tool of choice on the Mac, MacWhisper, got another major update today with real-time meeting transcripts, significantly improved speaker recognition, tighter integration with Apple Intelligence, and a new transcription model. Here are the details.

MacWhisper gets deeper Apple Intelligence integration

I’ve written in the past about how much I rely on MacWhisper, particularly as part of my podcast production workflow.

MacWhisper was one of the first AI-powered transcription tools for the Mac. Since indie developer Jordi Bruin launched it in 2023, it has been on a relentless streak of improvements and expanded support for new models, services, and workflows.

That has included everything from automatic meeting recording and speaker recognition to watched folders, system-wide dictation, local and cloud AI models, and integrations with services such as Notion, Zapier, Obsidian, and n8n.

Today, MacWhisper was updated to version 15.2, introducing an improved speaker recognition powered by NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Diarization model, which was announced just hours ago.

It supports up to 8 speakers and can also be used during live meetings in the new realtime meeting view!

Which brings us to another major addition in today’s update: real-time meeting transcriptions.

This feature had been sitting near the top of MacWhisper’s public roadmap for a while, and it is now here, allowing users to follow, refer back to, copy, or transfer a live transcript as the meeting unfolds.

You can keep the window above your other apps to follow along, and your recording and transcript are saved when the meeting ends.

When it comes to the actual transcription models, MacWhisper 15.2 adds Alibaba’s QWEN3-ASR transcription model with support for 22 languages, in addition to a tighter integration with Apple Intelligence, Siri, Spotlight, and Shortcuts on macOS 27.

Now, users running macOS (including in the EU) can search for transcripts system-wide, open them with Siri, pull their text into Shortcuts, and refer to the transcript currently on screen in Siri or Apple Intelligence requests.

Finally, MacWhisper 15.2 adds folders and subfolders for organizing transcripts and meetings, with support for dragging existing transcriptions into them from the sidebar.

To learn more about MacWhisper 15.2, follow this link.

title: iOS 27.2: New features, release date, more
snippet: Apple has kicked off beta testing of iOS 27.2, and the update brings several notable changes and new features. Here’s everything you need to know about iOS 27.2, which will likely be released to iPhone users as soon as next month. more…
fullText:
Apple has kicked off beta testing of iOS 27.2, and the update brings several notable changes and new features. Here’s everything you need to know about iOS 27.2, which will likely be released to iPhone users as soon as next month.

Why iOS 27.2 and not iOS 27.1?

Apple released iOS 27 on September 14, bringing a ton of new iPhone features, including Siri AI. iOS 27.2 entered beta testing just two days later on September 16.

What happened to iOS 27.1?

Apple previously confirmed that iPhone Duo will ship with iOS 27.1 when it’s released on October 23. This means iOS 27.1 includes many references to the iPhone Duo in its code, which Apple wants to keep under wraps until the device ships. iOS 27.1 will therefore be exclusive to the iPhone Duo.

The software paths for iPhone Duo and other iPhone models will then converge, either with an iOS 27.2.x software update or perhaps with iOS 27.3.

So, things will be awkward for a little bit, but everything will eventually return to normal.

iOS 27.2 new features

Redesigned Health app

At the iPhone 18 Pro event, Apple showcased an all-new version of the Health app that it said would be coming later this year. That new app has entered beta testing as part of iOS 27.2.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

The new Health app likely won’t be released with iOS 27.2 next month. Instead, this is Apple kicking off beta testing of the new app before ultimately releasing it to everyone later this year.

Read more: iOS 27.2 introduces Apple Health app overhaul, here’s what’s new

Profiles in the TV app

The Apple TV app in iOS 27.2 adds support for profiles for the first time. This feature has been available on tvOS for several years, but this is the first time it has come to iPhone.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

More Siri AI languages

Siri AI is the big new feature in iOS 27, and iOS 27.2 expands the feature to even more users. The update adds Siri AI support for the following languages:

French

Japanese

Korean

Portuguese

Spanish

Dual Capture mode for Group FaceTime

In iOS 27, Apple added a new Dual Capture feature for FaceTime that lets you have your front and rear cameras active at the same time. The person on the other end of the call will see you as well as whatever you’re looking at. iOS 27.2 expands this feature to Group FaceTime calls for the first time.

Dual Capture requires an iPhone 17 or later, and everyone on the call needs to be running iOS 27.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Odds and ends

In Apple Podcasts, the “Up Next” queue has been renamed to “New Episodes.” The “Continue Playing” section is directly below New Episodes. Episode lists also now use color-matched backgrounds based on the podcast art.

In the Music app, some of the red icons and accents have been changed to black.

iOS 27’s Call Context feature, which surfaces information right on your screen when calling a business, has been expanded to include anniversaries.

There are small changes to the alarms interface in the Clock app, such as smaller text for the AM and PM labels.

Hints at more features to come

Finally, iOS 27.2 code hints at a handful of other new features that could come soon to iPhone users. This includes live countdowns for new album releases in Apple Music, third-party app support for Describe a Shortcut, and new themes for CarPlay Ultra. iOS 27.2 also shows Apple is continuing its work on an anti-snatching feature for iPhone.

These features aren’t live in iOS 27.2 just yet, but the code suggests they are in active development inside Apple.

iOS 27.2 release date

iOS 27.2 is expected to be released to iPhone users sometime in October. Apple promised that Siri AI would come to new languages in October, and iOS 27.2 adds those new languages, so the update needs to be released before November for Apple to hit that promise.

Wrap up

Are you running the iOS 27.2 beta? Have you found any useful new features? What do you think of the new Health app? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Review: Beats 360 are the closest Apple headphones to AirPods Max, with one caveat
snippet: The highly anticipated Beats 360 are now available for purchase. After being teased prior to the World Cup, Apple’s latest pair of Beats headphones are now on the market. I got an early hands-on with them, and they’re quite an interesting product offering that I’ve thoroughly enjoyed using – though they have one key flaw: no wired connectivity, which will bother some more than others. more…
fullText:
The highly anticipated Beats 360 are now available for purchase. After being teased prior to the World Cup, Apple’s latest pair of Beats headphones are now on the market. I got an early hands-on with them, and they’re quite an interesting product offering that I’ve thoroughly enjoyed using – though they have one key flaw: no wired connectivity, which will bother some more than others.

Product overview

First things first, the Beats 360 come in at $349.99. At that price, they’re leaning towards the high end of the market, though they still fall well below the AirPods Max at $549. Alongside this launch, the existing Beats Studio Pro are being permanently reduced to a new price of $299.99. Of course, you can find them much cheaper at retailers: they currently run $169.95 on Amazon.

If you’ve been following Beats launches, you’ll know that they sometimes use Apple H1 or H2 chips, and sometimes they use custom Beats silicon. The Beats 360 do use Beats silicon, however there’s one key upgrade here: they now finally support automatic device switching with your Apple Account, Hey Siri support, as well as proper Find My integration. If you’re an Apple fan who’s been eyeing Beats as a more affordable version of AirPods Max, the Beats 360 are closer than ever to providing a true Apple experience. I was certainly pleased when I learned this.

There is one loss compared to most high-end headphones: there’s no automatic pausing when you take them off your head. You learn to live with it, though it takes some time to get used to.

Compared to Beats Studio Pro, the Beats 360 get 12dB louder, and offer 1.75x more active noise cancellation. They also support Adaptive EQ in iOS 27, and are the first Beats headphones to be IPX4 sweat and water resistant. Both offer spatial audio with dynamic head tracking, and the Beats 360 last around 8 hours longer than Beats Studio Pro with ANC turned on.

Beats 360 come in four colors: Cloud, Sky, Black, and Pink. I’ve personally been trying out the Sky’s, but they’re all pretty elegant colors.

Customization

The headlining feature of Beats 360 is their customizable design. You can easily swap out the ear cushions and head cushion for different color options. The ear cushions also have two variants, UltraPlush and Performance Knit. The former will be more comfortable for everyday wear, whereas the latter is better for working out.

Each set of cushions is available for $49.99, though there’s a launch promo while supplies last where you can pick them up for just $9.99. This is an incredible promo for those who want to customize their headphones based on their outfit, or to match their mood. I’d personally take advantage of it.

Customization is really the name of the game with Beats 360. With the four base color options, as well as eight additional cushion options, there are 32 total ways you can mix up your Beats 360. If you mix headband cushions from the earcups, there are up to 256 different options.

You can truly make these headphones yours – which is quite fun. Another advantage to this is the fact that when your ear cushions wear down, you can easily swap them out instead of calling the headphones a loss.

Plethora of Beats 360 color combos
My personal Beats 360 color combo

9to5Mac’s Take

The Beats 360 are good headphones for most Apple enthusiasts. If you’re looking to switch away from your AirPods Max to something lighter and more comfortable, I’d say these fit those criteria pretty well, though you’re taking a hit on sound quality. I’d also highly recommend picking up an UltraPlush cushion kit, as I personally find the fabric ones a bit uncomfortable for casual use. With the launch promo for cushion kits, there isn’t much reason not to.

As someone who primarily used AirPods Pro 3 prior to testing out the Beats 360, I’ve actually found myself to much prefer the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is solid, transparency didn’t disappoint, and the fact that they fold down flat didn’t make them too much of a hurdle to fit in my everyday backpack. Of course, earbuds will simply be more convenient for many scenarios, but I found myself missing these headphones when I was away from home (as I couldn’t wear them outdoors during review), which I’ve never really thought for any pair of over-ears in the past.

Frankly, the only major complaint I have with the Beats 360 is that they don’t support wired connectivity. There’s no headphone jack, and USB-C seemingly doesn’t support it either. This is a little bit of an inconvenience if you’re looking to use them in an environment that doesn’t play super nicely with Bluetooth, such as an airplane or with a game console.

Regardless of that, I truly adore what Beats has done with the customizable design. These have been some of my favorite headphones I’ve tested out, even compared to AirPods Max, which I could never get comfortable with because of their weight. Beats 360 have no comfort issues whatsoever, so long as I use the UltraPlush cushions.

Pricing & availability

Beats 360 are launching at $349.99, with deliveries and in-store availability beginning September 24th. You can order them on Amazon and at Apple.com.

The limited-time $9.99 cushion kit promo is available in the US, Canada, the UK, France, China, Australia, and South Korea. It’s valid through October 31st, while supplies last.

title: Apple hit with $5.7 billion verdict over Taptic Engine patent infringement
snippet: Apple must pay $5.7 billion for infringing on patents held by Taction Technology, a US jury ruled on Friday. The patents relate to Apple’s Taptic Engine, which is the hardware Apple uses to provide haptic feedback for notifications, button presses, and other interactions. Taction first filed the lawsuit in 2021, alleging Apple had “infringed and continues to infringe, directly and indirectly” its patents. more…
fullText:
Apple must pay $5.7 billion for infringing on patents held by Taction Technology, a US jury ruled on Friday. The patents relate to Apple’s Taptic Engine, which is the hardware Apple uses to provide haptic feedback for notifications, button presses, and other interactions.

Taction first filed the lawsuit in 2021, alleging Apple had “infringed and continues to infringe, directly and indirectly” its patents.

As reported by CNBC, the lawsuit centered around two patents:

U.S. Patent No. 10,659,885

U.S. Patent No. 10,820,117

Both patents are focused on a “vibration module for applying vibrational tractions to a wearer’s skin.” Taction argued that Apple’s Taptic Engine infringes upon its patents, saying that Apple was “capitalizing on Taction’s innovation and success.”

Apple’s Taptic Engine first debuted as part of the Apple Watch in 2014 and came to the iPhone 6s and iPhone 6s Plus the following year, replacing the older vibration motor.

In a statement, an Apple spokesperson said:

“While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today’s verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts.

Apple’s Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction’s technology, which Taction’s own testing of Apple’s products confirmed during trial. Apple does not use Taction’s technology, and we will appeal.”

Taction Technology is a California-based company that describes itself as being “obsessed by sound.” The company says that its “Transporter Technology powers the game-changing Corsair HS60 Haptic headphones, and will soon be powering other premium headphones from major manufacturers.”

In a statement to CNBC, Taction’s lead counsel said:

“We’re happy the jury found for Taction and vindicated its patent rights. Taction waited five and a half years for this case to get to trial, so it was a long time coming.”

You can read the original complaint for patent infringement filed by Taction here and Friday’s jury ruling here.

title: What do you actually use a laptop for, and would Googlebook be able to do it? [Poll]
snippet: Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced. more…
fullText:
Following a mediocre teaser back in May, Googlebook is officially here and, well, I’m still pretty skeptical. I’m not sure I see Google’s vision of this new lineup or laptops because, frankly, I’m not solving any of the problems Chromebooks already faced.

Our initial coverage of Googlebook is live, with Abner, Jordan, and Damien all walking away with a good first impression of Google’s efforts.

Google fully details Googlebooks: $899+, October launch, & more

Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid

Googlebook hands-on: What makes a laptop, a laptop? [Video]

Yet, I’m unconvinced thus far. I’ve yet to get my hands on a Googlebook and, as someone sitting mostly in the same boat as you, our readers, I’m yet to be sold on this new platform. I simply don’t understand why it exists, even more so why Google seems to think it will succeed.

Google’s entire pitch around why you should buy a Googlebook more or less boils down to smartphone integration – specifically Android integration. Googlebook takes existing tools from ChromeOS and supercharges them, giving you the ability to mirror apps, sync files, and do a whole lot more between your Android phone and your laptop. And it does sound pretty good! As someone who currently juggles a MacBook with various Android phones, there are integrations I wish existed; instant hotspot and proper Quick Share support (AirDrop works, but tends to be wildly slow) are at the top of that list. 

	

Googlebook is delivering the MacBook + iPhone experience, just for Android users. That’s the pitch.

Where it falls flat for me is in the apparent functionality. At its core, Googlebook is Android, just with a desktop experience built on top. The core stuff is there – desktop-class Chrome browser, customizable desktop, keyboard shorts, the lot. But the app ecosystem is built around Android apps, web apps, and Linux apps. The same core as ChromeOS, just with a different priority and with better performance on the Android app side, as Abner and Damien both noticed.

That’s where I’m struggling to get on board.

There’s plenty you can do on a Googlebook, sure, just like there was plenty you could do on a Chromebook. But you’re still making a trade-off. Google pointed out that around 70% of things people do on a laptop are done through their browser (Chrome, of course). And, yeah, I’d say that’s about how much I do in the browser on my Windows desktop or my MacBook. That other 30%, though, is the “make or break” that eventually broke me on ChromeOS. For me, it largely came down to Adobe’s apps which, as it stands, still aren’t replicated on Googlebook. On Google’s own website, the company touts a Googlebook’s ability to use Photoshop and Lightroom, but that’s just with the mobile apps – not the full-featured apps you can use on you know, most other laptops. 

Google knows people use these apps; otherwise, it wouldn’t take up a place on this site in the first place – the same goes for games, where Google advertises tons of popular titles like Forza Horizon, Marvel Rivals, Arc Raiders, and more, with only two of the games shown running natively and the rest delivered via GeForce Now.

The market has pretty clearly spoken in this regard. Chromebooks are out. There are remarkably few consumer-focused Chromebooks on the market today and, especially on the high end, it seems like hardly anyone is buying them – Google itself gave up on first-party Chromebooks over five years ago. 

To me at least, the reasoning seems obvious. When Chromebooks hit their stride, the market was full of compromises everywhere. There was no one perfect answer. But that’s changed in recent years. Apple’s M-series chips ushered in a new era for the MacBook which, in turn, influenced some major improvements across Windows laptops. Fast forward to today and there’s no lack of powerful, battery-efficient, thin & light laptop options and, despite “RAMageddon” ruining the price side of things, there’s been a huge push for more affordable machines in the wave of MacBook Neo and its clones – and those are very popular too. Giving up access to a full collection of full-featured apps for a lightweight operating system that gets roughly the same battery life for roughly the same price is a no-brainer, which means that Chromebooks are relegated to a niche. In enterprise/schools, for more affordable machines, for low-end hardware, ChromeOS still makes a lot of sense, but it’s a tough sell basically anywhere else, so you might be able to see why I’m so confused by Googlebook.

Googlebook’s pitch, again, isn’t bad, but does it make sense in today’s market? Who’s buying a laptop that’s inherently (and inarguably) restricted in what it can do, especially at a time when laptops are wildly inflated in price in the first place due to component shortages? 

This is the part where I turn the floor over to you.

Do you think Googlebook has stuck the landing? Has Google’s pitch resonated with you? 

	

Even more so, what are you using a laptop for in the first place? That’s perhaps the most important question around this. As mentioned, I’m personally using my laptop mostly in Chrome, with non-Chrome apps including the likes of Photoshop/Lightroom/Premiere, Spotify, Slack, and a handful of assorted other tools. There are a few of those I can replace – Spotify’s tablet interface should be a treat on a laptop, though I think Slack will be awful given how the Android app lacks any semblance of big-screen optimizations (on Android, as they’re immediately giving Apple something better), so maybe the Linux app will be better.

That’s just me. There are infinite ways people use their laptop. So, looking at what you do today, do you think a Googlebook can do it all? Vote in the poll below, then leave a comment.

title: I Tested Ninja’s CrushBoss, a $230 Blender That Chops, Dices, Minces and Mixes
snippet: The food processor and blender attachments are handy, while other elements feel like overkill.
fullText:
One of the biggest roadblocks for adding countertop appliances to your kitchen is storage. For folks with a small kitchen, myself included, the struggle often looks like a constant shuffle, trading one appliance for another in the pantry. This problem is less noticeable in larger kitchens, but you might end up with more clutter than you’d like.

This modestly sized blender does far more than blend.  John Carlsen/CNET

Eventually, you need to decide if you’ll use an appliance often enough to justify getting it. In my case, I’m much more likely to choose a multipurpose product like an Instant Pot pressure cooker or an air fryer. Perhaps this is why I was excited to test out the Ninja CrushBoss, which combines a large blender, food processor and small smoothie blender into a single device. I spent the two weeks using a sample unit from Ninja in my kitchen, and I’m eager to share my thoughts. 

Four appliances in one. Well, kind of

The main appeal of the Ninja CrushBoss is that it comes with three vessels: a 72-ounce blender pitcher, a 64-ounce food processor bowl and a 26-ounce smoothie tumbler.

CrushBoss isn’t Ninja’s first attempt at an all-in-one kitchen system, as the Ninja Detect, Ninja Professional Plus and Ninja Foodi Power Blender all attempt similar feats. What sets Ninja CrushBoss apart are the PrecisionDice and MultiBlade Disc attachments for the food processor bowl, plus a better smoothie tumbler design than previous models.

			

More from CNET

Similarly, the blender’s preset programs change depending on which vessel you attach to the 1850-watt base motor, with each program running automatically to achieve the desired results. You can rotate the outer ring of the small LCD screen to choose your setting, then make the final selection by pressing the top of the screen inward to click. It’s not a touchscreen, but it’s easy enough to use once you learn the controls.

Intelligent blending features, PrepIQ and SmoothSense, track the type and consistency of what you’re blending, but I didn’t notice a difference compared to the preset programs or custom speed controls.John Carlsen/CNET

There isn’t much that’s special about the large blender pitcher, which uses largely the same design as other standalone Ninja blenders. It comes with a single blade assembly and presets for mincing, small chopping and large chopping. The smoothie tumbler is similarly simple, with its small blade assembly supporting ice crushing, blending and smoothie presets. Compared to older tumblers, the Travel Tumbler’s main upgrade is a better carrying handle, flip-top lid and a large smoothie straw — it’s more like a Stanley cup than a NutriBullet personal blender.

Last, but not least, is the food processor, which has the most accessories, including a chopping blade, dough blade, MultiBlade Disc and the PrecisionDice assembly. Where the Ninja Detect’s food processor included reversible stainless steel discs, the MultiBlade attachment is largely plastic, with specific inserts depending on the model you choose. The model I tested came with inserts for thick slices, crinkle-cut slices and shredding — Ninja also sells inserts for thin slices, french fries and julienning.

While I understand that the plastic MultiBlade Disc and inserts reduce the amount of stainless steel in the package, I can’t help but wonder about their long-term durability compared to all-metal discs.John Carlsen/CNET

I call it a kind of four-in-one appliance because the smoothie tumbler’s main benefits are, naturally, smoother blending consistency than the large pitcher and greater travel portability with the included lid and smoothie straw. You can still use the large pitcher for family-size smoothies and anything too big for the other two vessels, so adding a blending function to each vessel is largely superfluous. Similarly, the dicing kit is hardly an appliance on its own, since you’ll see it on other food processor brands like KitchenAid and Breville.

How useful is the Ninja CrushBoss?

My Ninja CrushBoss tests were informal, so I mostly wanted to see whether it could handle a few tasks, like making salads, smoothies, processing cheese and chopping a few kinds of vegetables. I tested every attachment and accessory in the box, with most receiving multiple tests.John Carlsen/CNET

Of the three vessels, I spent the most time with the food processor. I used the PrecisionDice attachment to prepare a fruit salad, which went very smoothly and had no issues with mango, watermelon, strawberries and pineapple. I pureed some blackberries with the food processor’s chopping blade to add more texture to the salad, though the smoothie attachment was ultimately a better option for crushing the blackberry seeds.

Next, I swapped the dicing attachment for the MultiBlade and sliced potatoes and cucumbers with the normal and crinkle-cut attachments. Again, the results were very good. Things were a little less consistent when I processed carrots and cabbage with the shredder for a quick coleslaw, as some bits of each remained unprocessed between the blade and lid. The amount of unprocessed vegetables was minimal, so I tossed them into a bowl of ramen instead of manually chopping them for the coleslaw.

The point of the cheese test was to find the food processor’s limits, so I’m happy to report the motor safety cutoff and error messages worked as intended when I stressed the unit too much.John Carlsen/CNET

To give the food processor a proper workout, I brought out the cheddar cheese, which I put through the shredder, slicer and dicer. As you might suspect, the cheese worked best with the shredder, with very little waste and no clogs. The other two attachments are less suitable for cheese, with the slicing disc producing passable slices. However, I clogged the dicing tool when I tried to make cheese cubes. I ultimately succeeded with some tiny cubes, but I don’t recommend it. 

	

			

	

			

									

						The Best Blenders We Tested in 2026					

							

		

While I didn’t use the dough blade attachment much, it seemed good for mixing bread dough into a state where I could knead it by hand. I ran three cycles using the dough preset — though I admit the last cycle was because I forgot to add an ingredient. One reason I finished by hand was that I could hear the motor straining a bit toward the end of the second and third cycles.

Even if I’m not 100% on board with using it for dense bread dough, the unit is plenty powerful for cookie dough and cake batter.John Carlsen/CNET

I suspect the CrushBoss can handle the job, as the manual says it can hold up to 2 pounds of dough and shut off if necessary, but it took only a minute of hand-kneading after processing to reach the consistency I wanted. My advice: Listen to your machine and avoid tasks that trigger the auto-shutoff too often. Fortunately, my testing didn’t surface any problems with the system’s durability.

Beyond the food processor bowl, little stood out about the blender pitcher and smoothie tumbler attachments. Each did well with various levels of blending, pureeing and ice crushing, but nothing so outstanding that my ancient Oster blender couldn’t also do. The biggest advantages over my modest blender are the pitcher’s size — even if it’s more than I need in my kitchen — and the tumbler’s portability. Ninja says CrushBoss isn’t suitable for hot blending, so you can’t safely use it with hot liquids.

The challenge of modular kitchen systems like Ninja CrushBoss

Somewhat paradoxically, the modular nature of the Ninja CrushBoss is also its biggest weakness — at least for me.John Carlsen/CNET

Although I’m happy that I don’t have to store three motorized bases for separate specialty appliances, all of Ninja’s vessels and attachments are bulky enough that they’d take up an entire shelf in my kitchen cabinets. There’s not really a safe way to store the extremely sharp food processor discs, so I ultimately kept them in a carrying case for a massage gun I threw out ages ago. Fortunately, you can safely store the largest blender blade assemblies in each vessel.

The other challenge is that while all of the attachments are dishwasher-safe, that only applies to the top rack. My older dishwasher’s top rack isn’t adjustable, so I can’t fit any of the vessels inside and I have to wash them all by hand. This isn’t a problem I experience with the glass jar of my Oster blender, or the slightly smaller vessel of the Tribest Backspin I tested in 2025. At least the other parts fit, which made cleanup much more manageable.

My point in calling these out isn’t to discourage anyone interested in the CrushBoss, but to note that storage space and dishwasher space still matter before you buy.

Should you buy the Ninja CrushBoss?

The CrushBoss’s value becomes more apparent as the amount of food increases.John Carlsen/CNET

As I used the Ninja CrushBoss 4-in-1, I kept coming back to one central question: “Who is this for?” Ultimately, it’s a harder question to answer than I thought. I have no problem recommending each function separately — blending, smoothies, dicing and food processing — because it seems to do all of these well enough.

For example, this particular setup should work well for two types of households: large families and meal preppers. I grew up in a large family, and having an appliance to prepare a huge amount of ingredients for every meal is a no-brainer. Another group that might benefit is the meal-prepper, regardless of household size.

Still, selling everything together in a single kit is excessive for someone like me, who has a small apartment. I have plenty of travel cups for smoothies and rarely need to process large amounts of food. Ninja thankfully offers various CrushBoss configurations and will most likely sell the attachments separately down the line, like with its older products. Personally, I’d love a configuration with only a large pitcher and food processor — I don’t need a smoothie tumbler.

At $320, the Ninja CrushBoss 4-in-1 costs about what you’d pay for separate Ninja appliances, but it is pricier than previous generations of Ninja’s modular kitchen systems, even without the dicing kit. This is a drop in the bucket compared to getting similar attachments for a Vitamix Ascent X. Despite my personal reservations, I think the Ninja CrushBoss 4-in-1 is a great idea, especially for folks looking to consolidate multiple specialty appliances into a single modular system. It taps into the reason why people love the classic KitchenAid stand mixer, and that’s a good thing.

title: Microsoft quietly ending ‘Copilot+ PC’ branding for Windows laptops
snippet: After a couple of years of relentlessly pushing it, Microsoft is seemingly ending its Copilot+ PC branding for Windows laptops. more…
fullText:
After a couple of years of relentlessly pushing it, Microsoft is seemingly ending its Copilot+ PC branding for Windows laptops.

Windows Central spoke with executives from Microsoft and Qualcomm about the lack of Copilot+ PC branding on the latest Surface machines. While it’s not been said explicitly, Surface CVP Brett Ostrum all-but-confirmed the end of that branding by saying:

…these are not called Copilot+ PCs. They do meet all the requirements of our previous bar for what Copilot+ devices are. We still lean into the narrative around AI on the edge and being able to have a hybrid solution out there.

Copilot+ PC branding was generally used to identify a laptop that met certain hardware requirements around AI features, particularly the NPU, which virtually every mid-high-end laptop already supports. Windows Central further points out that Nvidia’s RTX Spark push has been absent of any mention of Copilot+ PC branding.

Microsoft started using this branding back in 2024, but when the flagship feature of the Copilot+ PC, Recall, was met with backlash, the branding became little more than a hardware checkbox that consumers didn’t fully understand. 

	

The only big question left – does this mean the Copilot Key is going away?

Apple says that AirPods firmware updates are automatically installed while your AirPods are charging and within Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac that’s connected to WiFi. You can check the firmware version of your AirPods in the Settings app on iPhone. 

Custom EQ comes to AirPods

Once you install the AirPods firmware update, you’ll see a long-awaited new feature in the Settings app: custom EQ.

You now have more control over how your AirPods sound thanks to the new custom EQ controls. In the Settings app, you can adjust the lows, mids, and highs of your AirPods sound.

“AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls,” Apple explains. “If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.”

While adjusting the custom EQ settings, you can play a song from Apple Music right in the Settings app to hear the adjustments in real time.

This isn’t the most advanced equalizer feature out there. It’s a basic, three-band system. Still, it’s a long-awaited AirPods feature that Apple has finally given users—even if most will likely stick with the default levels.

You can find the new custom EQ feature in the AirPods section of the Settings app under the “Audio and Routing” menu. The feature is available on all AirPods with an H2 chip, including AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4, and AirPods Max 2.

Other iOS 27 features for AirPods

Here are the other new AirPods features for iOS 27:

Settings app redesign: In iOS 27, Apple has redesigned the AirPods interface in the Settings app. The controls have been reorganized, with separate menus for Hearing Health, Find My, Live Translation, and more.

Adaptive Audio slider: In the Settings app, you now have a slider to further fine-tune Adaptive Audio mode.

GymKit: While GymKit has been around for years, it’s always required an Apple Watch. As my colleague Zac explains, iOS 27 brings the full GymKit experience to iPhone and AirPods Pro 3.

Precision Finding: You can now use Precision Finding in the Find My app on Apple Watch to locate AirPods Pro 3.

Siri AI: When paired to a compatible iPhone, AirPods can interact with Siri AI.

Wrap up

What new AirPods features are you most excited to try? Are you going to try the new custom EQ feature? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Android Auto rolls out game support, no longer in beta
snippet: Google is graduating game support on Android Auto from a limited beta to broad availability, allowing developers to bring games to your car’s display. more…
fullText:
Google is graduating game support on Android Auto from a limited beta to broad availability, allowing developers to bring games to your car’s display.

First available last year, games in Android Auto and Android Automotive bring a bit of interactive fun to the car’s display. While there’s no direct integration with things like the car’s steering wheel, it’s a nice way to add something fun to the biggest screen in your vehicle for times you might be stuck on the side of the road, waiting on an EV to charge, or other times where the vehicle is not moving.

Around 30 games are available on Android Auto today, but that list is likely to start expanding soon.

Google announced this week that game support on Android Auto is no longer in beta, meaning that game support is open to all developers rather than requiring specific approval from Google. 

	

Google says:

Bringing your game to cars lets you reach users in their vehicles during natural downtime, such as while waiting at a charging station or for a curbside order pickup. Today’s milestone means that we’re opening up access so developers can now publish games to the open testing and production tracks on Google Play. In this post, we’ll cover how to adapt your existing Android game for the car screen, focusing on key technical requirements and publishing criteria.

Android games must declare support for Android Auto and Android Automotive OS – they’re separate declarations behind the scenes, and there are many more games that support Android Automotive without Android Auto support as it stands today.

Games on Android Auto should be able to adapt to different display sizes and need to recognize when a vehicle is parked or not – games can only be played if the vehicle is parked. Games can also support controllers on Android Auto and Android Automotive. 

Google’s full documentation on what developers need to do can be found here.

title: Nothing Phone (4a) and (3a) Pro can now join Android 17 open beta
snippet: Right on schedule, Nothing is releasing Nothing OS 5.0 open beta for the Phone (4a), Phone (3a Pro, and Phone (3a) before the company’s official Android 17 release next month. more…
fullText:
Right on schedule, Nothing is releasing Nothing OS 5.0 open beta for the Phone (4a), Phone (3a Pro, and Phone (3a) before the company’s official Android 17 release next month.

The Android 17 package contains a few changes for Nothing phones. It was first released as a beta update for the Nothing Phone (3) with visual changes to the system UI and animations across the board. The update also includes new widgets, updates to the camera app, and a dedicated Glyph app for light controls and features.

You can check out the full changelog in our previous coverage. At its core, it brings Nothing’s devices up to date with the latest version of Android. Of course, this company is known for creating its own spin on both hardware and software.

Right now, though, Nothing is actively rolling out Android 17 beta access to the Nothing Phone (4a), Phone (3a) Pro, and Phone (3a). The update leaves out the Phone (3a) Lite, which is expected to get access later in the year. Users with either of those devices should now be able to access the Nothing OS 5.0 open beta, which puts it on par with the Phone (3).

	

In terms of scheduling, Nothing is right on time. The company posted its release schedule when the first open beta rolled out, and it remains unchanged. The three devices announced today will be followed by the Phone (2a) and Phone (2a) Plus in October.

The same post also notes the Phone (4a) and Phone (3a) series will be pushed to the official Android 17 build in early November. The rollout is expected to end sometime in January 2027.

For the time being, Phone (4a) and (3a) series users should now be able to access Nothing OS 5.0 in its early stages.
