fullText:
In Control Resonant, the entire world is at stake. But that didn’t stop the diligent employees of the Federal Bureau of Control from filing reams of paperwork, and it didn’t stop me from reading everything I could find, either. Reading is often optional in Resonant, but it’s where some of the game’s best details — and even love stories! — can be found.

In the world of Control Resonant and its predecessor, 2019’s Control, the FBC deals with mysterious, otherworldly objects and entities that defy explanation. But the FBC itself is still an old-school bureaucratic agency, and that means tons of (often heavily redacted) reports and memos and miscellaneous bits of paper to sort through. I like reading, and I especially like reading Remedy’s clever and often funny writing, but I was overwhelmed at first by the sheer amount of text.

Initially I skipped documents that seemed optional: the enemy logs, which are compiled in a separate tab and unlocked automatically after fighting each enemy type for the first time. I was kind of busy just learning how to get around — I’m not the best at spatial reasoning in general, and gravity doesn’t always matter in Resonant’s M.C. Escher-ified version of Manhattan. I was also too busy beating down the game’s many Hiss and mold enemies to read about them.

But I was having enough trouble with combat early on that I eventually decided to read through the enemy logs I’d unlocked to see if they’d be any help. (There’s an assist mode so you can tweak the combat difficulty, but I was feeling too stubborn to use it. Remedy has since deployed a hotfix to address criticisms of the combat balance.) The logs, compiled by the FBC’s “Threat Assessment Team,” did actually help; they detail each enemy’s attack patterns and weaknesses, which aren’t always easy to figure out when they come at you in large groups. But I was delighted to find that the enemy logs also hide a workplace romantic comedy.

The Threat Assessment Team consists of Rick Patel, who documents the Hiss, and Lydia M.B. McPierce, who documents the mold and some later-game enemies. Rick is pretty serious and straightforward, whereas Lydia finds lots of time to talk shit about the mold in between her regular notes. Opposites attract, though. Across dozens of logs, I saw their individual personalities unfold — as well as the beginning of their love story.

One of the enemies, the Hiss Transporter, is a city bus that’s been corrupted by the Hiss and sends out drones to attack on its behalf. In his log about it, Rick describes the dynamic between the bus and its drones — which are seemingly once-human Hiss entities fused to bus seats — as “motherly.” Lydia calls him out on this in a separate document about a mold enemy called the Spore Mother. “(For the record, I was not the one who named this one ‘mother,’ that was Rick. I went to therapy and did the work precisely so I wouldn’t feel the urge to do that),” she writes in an aside at the bottom. In another document, Lydia teases Rick, who she’s calling “Ricky” at this point, about beating him at chess and challenges him to a rematch.

Lydia is one of the best examples in Resonant of how funny Remedy’s writing can be, while Rick is much drier. But he’s also sweet and references Lydia often; in one log, he says that had he realized Lydia had emetophobia, he would’ve offered to trade some responsibilities with her so she could avoid the vomit-like attacks of the mold. (I have emetophobia myself, so I found this especially charming. Good on Ricky.) Then, in a document about a particularly dangerous Hiss variant that he came too close to during his observations, Rick finally lays it all bare:

I could have died. Another close call like that and it might just be the end for me. I don’t want to go without taking a chance on us, Lydia. Remember how we laughed at our ideal dates being the exact opposites of each other, how chaotic a pair we’d make? It doesn’t have to be just a joke. I think we could have something real together, you and I. What do you think? (Don’t worry, you can tell me over coffee what a coward I am for not doing this in person.)

I’m not sure if Lydia has actually seen this note, because I’m still missing one singular enemy log. But I know she likes him back. In a late-game document, as the world is really looking doomed, Lydia adds an aside at the bottom: “(Hey Ricky, this is out of left field, but if we actually survive this, wanna grab a coffee sometime?)”

Remedy seeds little stories and fun details like these throughout the world of Resonant, not just in written documents. But reading, it turns out, was integral to my experience. I learned how to fight the game’s enemies a little better, and in the process, I was endeared to two characters I never actually met. There’s also a lot more to discover than just office romance — everything from an influencer’s view of Manhattan’s “inception ahh streets” to the FBC’s serious ethics violations — and so much of it enriches Remedy’s fantastically weird world.

I’m now determined to track down and kill that last enemy type so I can read Lydia’s final log, and I’m sure I’ll stumble upon some other documents I missed along the way. I can’t wait to see what I find.

fullText:
Earlier this month, Pokémon card content creator Natalie Roush posted a video to her YouTube and Instagram pages that enraged the larger collection community. In the now-deleted video, Roush shows off two premium boxes of cards that had not yet been officially released, and implores viewers not to be mad. But they were; other creators claimed that cards Roush had purchased were stolen from the manufacturer and mocked her for trying to sell them at exorbitant prices. The Roush situation was a high-profile example of the way Pokémon card collecting culture has been upended by the influencer economy and people trying to profit off the hobby. Though Roush has been relatively quiet in the days since the blowup, Pokémon collectors have been up in arms over a different — but very much related — problem.

When the Pokémon Trading Card Game’s long-awaited 30th Celebration set finally released last week, collectors across the country lined up outside of stores in hopes of getting their hands on some shiny pieces of cardboard. The anniversary set has unusually strong pull rates — the rate at which you’re likely to find rare “chase” cards in a given set — giving more fans the cards they’ve always dreamed of, and potentially upsetting the aftermarket Poké-conomy. Some diehard Poké-fans even camped out overnight because a resurgence in popularity has made the cards much more difficult to find and buy in person. But another group of Pokémon card hunters was able to secure the highly sought-after set without having to travel to physical retailers or navigate the online Pokémon Center.

Those people — resellers who often use automated bots to buy dozens of boxes of cards as soon as they’re available for preorder online — might not have had any intention of collecting the 30th Celebration set for themselves. But they have been trying to offload their spoils at marked-up prices to fans who haven’t had a chance to buy cards for themselves. Most retailers can’t keep cards on shelves, but there are plenty of videos online of resellers showing off piles of product they were able to obtain either by placing orders with bots or using inventory checking programs that alert them when brick-and-mortar stores receive stock. It’s also easy to find footage of resellers getting into altercations over cards, and in one recent instance, a 72-year-old man was arrested and charged with a first-degree misdemeanor for tracking a Pokémon delivery worker’s location with a device secretly planted in her car.

Though flipping trading cards is nothing new, the Pokémon reselling economy has gotten much bigger in recent years as people have taken note of how durable the franchise’s popularity is. Many resellers like BotterBoyNova started off with other kinds of valuable merchandise before realizing that Pokémon products can be sold for far beyond the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, or MSRP. When I spoke with Nova recently, he told me that — like many millennials — he’s been a Pokémon fan since the mid-’90s. Nova was originally a content creator whose videos were mostly focused on reselling sneakers, but seeing how easy it was to profit from reselling Pokémon products convinced him that he needed to get in on the action.

“Resellers in what’s described as the ‘Sneaker Twitter’ space are tapped in with practically every category of collectible that can resell for a profit,” Nova explained to me via Discord. “It’s not a situation where I’m singling out the Pokémon card market. It just so happens that it’s highly profitable and difficult to purchase for MSRP, and those are the conditions that our community specializes in.”

Rather than operating independently, Nova works with Polar Chefs — a “cook group” community that sells monthly subscriptions to a variety of reseller tools and services. Subscriptions range from $660 per year to $75 per month, and they come with access to Polar Chefs’ private Discord server, restock alerts, and a selection of bots that can be used to buy cards. These bots make it easy for people to create multiple accounts on retailers’ websites that are attached to virtual credit cards, while the buyer’s IP address is spoofed with proxies. Technically, this kind of process isn’t illegal — at least not yet; Congress outlawed concert ticket-focused bots in 2016 and lawmakers have proposed doing the same for retail bots. But it does violate most retailers’ terms of service, which is why some resellers’ orders are canceled.

Retail bots aren’t illegal, but they do violate most retailers’ terms of service.

Using Polar Chefs’ tools, Nova has been able to purchase massive amounts of Pokémon cards at MSRP from various retailers without being blocked by websites’ anti-bot security measures. Nova described his process of securing cards with bots as being “almost completely hands free,” and explained that the real work doesn’t begin until he has to sort and sell his inventory to a couple of bulk buyers.

“During most weeks, I spend less than 3-5 hours a week on the reselling side of things (setting up bots, buying inventory, selling and fulfilling inventory),” Nova said, noting that he’s commonly asleep while pre-programmed bots make purchases for him. “I wait for notifications to come in from Polar Chefs which inform me of releases, bot adjustments I need to make, etc.”

Though it is difficult to pinpoint exactly when Pokémon reselling really exploded in the past few years, the rise of groups like Polar Chefs feels reflective of the way that the creator economy evolved during the covid-19 pandemic. Resellers like Nova are influencers whose videos are designed to sell people on the idea that they could also be making money by flipping cards at scale. And monetized cook groups are prime examples of how online hustle culture has become more focused on the sale of how-to guides and courses for practices that can be seen as morally suspect.

There’s an argument to be made that the scarcity created by resellers is part of what has driven the popularity of platforms like Whatnot — an online marketplace where people can pay for things like sealed Pokémon products, which are then opened on livestreams by the seller before they’re sent to the buyer. Many Whatnot streamers present themselves as entrepreneurs who are providing their audiences with a helpful service while also entertaining them. But the platform has been accused of operating more like an illegal gambling operation, and there is an entire ecosystem of creators whose content documents Whatnot streamers scamming their customers.

But with the 30th Celebration packs flooding the market with rare cards, the scammers could be out of luck. Over the past week, X and Reddit have been inundated with screenshots from unnamed Discord servers where people claiming to be resellers appear to be melting down over not being able to sell their overpriced cards. One of the more widely circulated images features a person insisting that resellers are “the people that actually ensure [The Pokémon Company] makes money,” while complaining that “there’s literally no value in these sets because everyone can pull the rare bullshit.” In another, a reseller says they are filing a class action lawsuit against The Pokémon Company “for independent vendors who suffered severe financial asset devaluation due to artificial market saturation.”

The absurdity of these posts suggests that they might have been written by people making fun of actual resellers, as does the fact that while searching Discord I found some posts that use the exact same wording. Those posters might have just been looking for attention, but the state of the larger reselling economy does seem to be having a negative impact on Pokémon cards’ availability.

Even though The Pokémon Company is printing more cards than ever, almost everything about the modern aftermarket economy has made it harder for ordinary people — especially children — to participate in the hobby. Nova told me that he thinks casual collectors who just want to pull cool cards for themselves are completely justified in feeling that resellers are making Pokémon less accessible. He also believes that collectors whose interest in the cards is “incentivized by monetary gain” are hypocrites for taking issue with resellers. Aside from actually playing with them, the real fun of Pokémon cards is in the hunt and delight when you’re able to find a pack that shocks you with its contents. It’s an experience everyone’s supposed to be able to enjoy, but it’s being ruined by hustlers.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 one week later: There’s so much more than meets the eye
snippet: When Apple unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12, two features stood out: the new Siri Recap feature, as well as the much improved heart rate monitor. While those two features were part of the reason I was compelled to buy the new Apple Watch, I’ve found myself delighted by much more than just those two things. more…
fullText:
When Apple unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12, two features stood out: the new Siri Recap feature, as well as the much improved heart rate monitor. While those two features were part of the reason I was compelled to buy the new Apple Watch, I’ve found myself delighted by much more than just those two things.

Battery and charging

While Apple’s website doesn’t quote any additional battery life for Apple Watch Series 12 compared to Series 11, the battery certainly feels like it lasts longer. As I’ve written in the past, I was someone who used the WHOOP prior to the Apple Watch Series 12, and even though I kept my Apple Watch, I never used it for sleep tracking.

After the keynote, I decided to give Apple Watch sleep tracking a shot. That said, on my Series 11, juggling sleep tracking and charging was a bit of a pain. After using the watch throughout the day, I’d have to charge it a little bit before going to sleep, then when I wake up, I’d have to charge it again.

On Series 12, that isn’t the case. It has enough battery to last through a day and overnight, and now I just charge it when I wake up. Apple Watch Series 12 also charges significantly faster, which makes that part less of a pain. 15 minutes of charging gets you up to 12 hours of use, per Apple.

I imagine the new S11 chip, derived from the A20 Pro’s 2nm design, is a large part of the reason why battery life feels so much longer. Regardless of the why, it feels amazing to not have charging anxiety around sleep tracking on the Apple Watch Series 12. Another big upside to the S11 chip? Apple Watch Series 12 feels so much faster, especially with Siri.

Software exclusives

On Series 12, Apple finally includes a proper step counter as a complication, which I like checking on in my smart stack. Could this come to older Apple Watches? Probably. It’s not like Apple didn’t count steps before. Apple Watch Series 12 certainly counts them more accurately, but given the fact that the data is there, I think Apple should just add the complication. Either way, it’s nice to have on Series 12.

Another neat new feature is the entire Readiness app, which gives you an idea of how okay you’re doing today based on last night’s sleep, your previous day’s activity, and your vitals. This is similar to a recovery score on WHOOP, and I was certainly happy to see Apple add this to the Apple Watch? It’s a bit of a bummer it’s exclusive to the Series 12, but I could understand why Apple isn’t willing to calculate it with less accurate data.

Wrap up

All in all, the Apple Watch Series 12 is a rather nice upgrade. It’s a total S year, but if you care about your Apple Watch actually doing more rather than just looking different, I’d say this might be one of the most substantial year over year upgrades since Apple Watch Series 4.

The bezels certainly got a slight bit thicker compared to Series 10 and 11. As someone who uses a watch face with a black background, I can’t say I’ve noticed this much – though I hope Apple improves on this in the next iteration.

One last thing of note: Apple Watch Series 12 offers Ceramic Shield 2 on the aluminum models, making it hold up to scratches much better than older Apple Watch models. I haven’t owned mine long enough to truly test this, though so far my Apple Watch still looks perfect.

title: This Comically Dark PSA Pushes Back Against Big Tech Enshittification
snippet: Cory Doctorow and the Norwegian Consumer Council are behind a hilarious and insightful ad campaign about how everything’s getting worse.
fullText:
Imagine, if you will, a pale figure of Death, dressed in a black robe holding a scythe, alongside a handsome, lumberjack-looking Nordic fella who goes by the name Enshittificator. As partners in crime, they conspire to make your life suck, all because they have the power to make digital products and services worse. 

If that piques your interest — and maybe sounds too much like real life — a new “anti-enshittification” ad campaign is worth a few minutes of your time.

The term “enshittification” was popularized in 2022 by author and activist Cory Doctorow, and its massive cultural surge earned it a place in Merriam-Webster’s slang hub last year. Enshittification is a deliberate process, designed by companies to maximize profit. 

			

More from CNET

It starts with luring you to a product or service, then making it so good that you become completely dependent on it. The next step is to pull the rug out from under you by hiding basic features behind a paywall, reducing overall quality and squeezing you for every last dime while providing as little value as possible. 

The Death and Enshittificator video above, released on YouTube in mid-September, is the second of a series from the Norwegian Consumer Council, an independent, government-funded nonprofit that advocates for consumer rights. The main character, the Enshittificator, is a bearded Nordic man who says in the first video, released in February, that his “job is to make things shitty.” 

The initial video concludes with Mr. Enshittificator getting into a car accident because he didn’t pay a subscription for his braking system, a scenario he appeared to find amusing. In the second video, he meets Death in the hospital, and the two enter into a business relationship. (He now dons a yellow hazmat suit to stay alive.) 

The duo spends time making every conceivable product worse, from TVs and toothbrushes to smartphone storage. They point out that products with long lifespans, like the famously indestructible Nokia 3310 — which makes a cameo appearance — only generate revenue once. If companies want a profitable business model, however, they have to use low-quality materials, ensure products can’t be fixed and stop issuing updates. 

“Look at all the companies that used to make solid products,” the Enshittificator said. “Where are they now?”

“Dead,” Death said, and they share a knowing smile. 

The Norwegian Consumer Council’s ads are part of its Breaking Free initiative, a multipronged policy approach to make technology work in favor of consumers, rather than against them. The campaign craftily relies on dark humor to detail how enshittification affects everyday life, from paid subscription models to planned obsolescence, which forces you to buy newer devices. 

The videos are also a strikingly accurate commentary on the dismal state of products and gadgets in the digital age. Prices go up while reliability plummets. Companies rely on shady advertising tactics and dodge consumer protection rights. 

Doctorow himself collaborated with the nonprofit to help launch the series, which he’s immensely pleased with. In an email to CNET, he said, “The idea that firms’ market power means that they can worsen their offerings with impunity, combined with the minor license to vulgarity of my dirty little word, have proven a winning combination for helping people direct their anger in the right direction.”

Real life (and death)

It would not be shocking if there were actual board rooms that looked like this.Norwegian Consumer Council

The enshittification process is relatable and real. In 2020, Apple agreed to pay up to $500 million to settle the landmark “batterygate” class action lawsuit over allegations that it secretly slowed down older iPhone models through software updates. Powerful tech companies have poured massive amounts of money into lobbying against right-to-repair laws, preventing customers from fixing their own devices when they break.  

“It’s really important that the products can’t be fixed,” said the Enshittificator. “It breaks, then it dies, so you have to buy a new one. And another one. And another one. And another one. And another one.”

“This way, we’re actually slowly killing the planet as well,” a smiling Death said, helpfully chiming in. 

The videos also satirize how digital services slowly degrade over time. In one scene, the Enshittificator tells an employee, “The 1,000 pictures of your deceased mother are mine, and you’re going to pay for them.” It’s a direct nod to Google Photos’ 2021 policy shift, which ended free unlimited storage and capped free accounts at 15GB, requiring users to get a subscription to keep already uploaded photos on the platform. 

Another scene takes a jab at automakers who sell you basic functionality as an add-on subscription service. 

“I don’t have any more money. You have me in the palm of your hand,” said the Enshittificator in a fake presentation about selling cars. “You can crush me. So what do you do? Updates. Radio? Premium feature. Heating? Premium feature. Now I have a shitty car, and I can’t afford a new one, but what I can afford is a small monthly payment!”

This is a reference to BMW’s controversial microtransaction model, where it tried to make heated seats and other in-car features part of a subscription plan. While intense consumer backlash forced the German automaker to walk back some of the “add-ons,” several features remain behind a paywall. Other brands have followed suit — Hyundai’s BlueLink and Kia Connect require paid plans to use remote start. For a period, both manufacturers even omitted the remote-start button from the physical key fob, completely blocking owners from using the feature for free.

Can it be fixed?

It’s important, though a little depressing, to imagine how much better life would be if companies actually invested money into making their products better, safer and longer-lasting — and not just more profitable for them. 

In its Breaking Free: Pathways to a Fair Technological Future report, the Norwegian Consumer Council argues that major tech business models “are often fundamentally incompatible with consumer and human rights.” To dismantle the “walled gardens run by Big Tech feudalists” and end dependence on Big Tech, the nonprofit is pushing for policy reforms built around a three-pronged strategy based on democratic values and principles of openness. 

The first is interoperability, which would force platforms to interface with one another. This is already taking shape under the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required Apple to allow third-party app stores and mandated Meta to support external chats in WhatsApp, 

Next comes portability, which would allow users to move their contacts, content, photos and anything else to rival services. A subscriber fed up with Spotify adding AI features, for instance, would be able to switch to YouTube Music or Apple Music without losing their saved playlists, thereby eliminating platform lock-in. 

Finally, and arguably the most difficult to implement, is decentralization of social media, which could shift social media away from single-entity corporate control toward open networks like the Fediverse (which powers platforms such as Mastodon). Though still evolving as protocols develop, decentralization enhances interoperability, making cross-network movement frictionless.

Reining in Big Tech remains an uphill battle, but in the meantime, the campaign offers a hilarious — and painfully accurate — look at the modern digital hellscape.

“The true mark of success for a project like this is when other people pick it up and run with it,” Doctorow said.

title: iPhone 18 Pro’s best Dynamic Island feature is one Apple barely mentioned
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro is here (read our review), and its Dynamic Island is better than ever. My personal favorite change is something Apple barely mentioned: an improved dual Live Activity mode. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro is here (read our review), and its Dynamic Island is better than ever. My personal favorite change is something Apple barely mentioned: an improved dual Live Activity mode.

Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 Pro lets you see more information when running two Live Activities

Apple debuted the Dynamic Island in 2022 on the iPhone 14 Pro. And while software support for Live Activities has expanded a lot since then, the actual Dynamic Island hardware has stayed unchanged.

But with iPhone 18 Pro, Apple managed to shrink the Dynamic Island for the first time. 

By moving certain Face ID components under the display, iPhone 18 Pro adds slightly more usable screen real estate than previous iPhones had. 

More importantly though, the Dynamic Island can now display more Live Activity information than before.

In Apple’s announcement earlier this month, it spotlighted how three Live Activities can now run at a time—up from the previous limit of two.

That’s a nice upgrade, but the change I’ve found even more beneficial (and I’m not alone) is that your second Live Activity can be a lot more informative on iPhone 18 Pro.

That’s because if you’re only running two Live Activities, there’s more space available than before, and Apple uses that space to give the second Live Activity additional info.

So if you’re listening to media while running a timer—something I do all the time at the gym—now you’ll actually see the remaining time in the Dynamic Island. Before, it only showed a timer icon.

I look forward to seeing how apps make their Live Activities even more useful for iPhone 18 Pro users.

French soccer legend Zinedine Zidane begins his tenure as Les Bleus’ head coach on Friday with a tricky first test in the UEFA Nations League away to Turkey.

Zidane has big boots to fill, succeeding his former teammate Didier Deschamps, who consistently led the French to the latter stages of major tournaments throughout his 14 years in charge, notably winning the World Cup in 2018.

title: Android’s Create My Widget ‘app’ detailed on phones, Googlebooks
snippet: Create My Widget will debut in early October on Googlebooks. Ahead of that, a Play Store listing details what the interface will look like, including on Android phones. more…
fullText:
Create My Widget will debut in early October on Googlebooks. Ahead of that, a Play Store listing details what the interface will look like, including on Android phones.

On phones, we see a guided creation experience with categories like:

Combo: Combine different or similar themed topics

Weather alerts: UV Conditions, Tide times, Wind forecast

My world clock: Timezones, Daylight savings countdown

Daily Brief: Horoscopes, Daily recipes, Facts, Affirmations 

Important dates: Countdown to birthdays, holidays, & anniversaries

Markets: Stocks, Crypto, Exchange rates

Each shows a carousel of suggested widgets, while you can always “describe your widget” with the prompt box at the bottom. The final step is to add it to your homescreen.

The Googlebook interface lists more categories like Weather, Sports & fitness, Events & travel, Daily habits, Important dates, Finance, and Tools & tips. Each is home to several “templates” that help teach users what is possible.

	

These generative widgets can make use of various Material 3 Expressive shapes for simpler, low-information designs.

The release date for Create My Widget is September 24, while the package name is straightforward enough: com.google.android.apps.yourwidget.

The version we have on the Play Store today is 1.27.983746769.0-desktop_release and focused on the upcoming Googlebook launch.

fullText:
Apple TV has been called “the new HBO” for its focus on quality over quantity. But recently, the streamer has starting ramping its lineup of shows I want to watch, and I can’t keep up.

Apple TV’s quality and quantity have ramped up as streamer hits new stride

I’ve subscribed to Apple TV since it first debuted in 2019, and the streamer has typically had 1-2 shows on at a time that I’ve wanted to watch.

This kind of output resembles HBO, which has built its brand creating fewer, but generally higher-quality shows than most competitors.

In the last couple years though, Apple’s output has been slowly growing, and at the same time its batting average has arguably improved too.

The result? Apple has too many good shows on right now, and I can’t keep up.

Currently airing every week on Apple TV are new episodes of:

Ted Lasso, one of my favorite shows

Slow Horses, another all-time best Apple series

Dark Matter, a sci-fi series I loved the first season of, yet haven’t started the second

Brothers, a new half-hour comedy with Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson that looks fun

Last Seen, a new thriller I’ve heard great things about but haven’t watched

plus Women in Blue and Knife Edge, both of which I might watch in a slower season but right now they’re low priorities

I’m excited to dive into Dark Matter, as season 1 made it one of my favorite sci-fi shows just behind Severance and Pluribus. But it’s been hard to find time to start season 2. And I’m always up for a comfort watch half-hour comedy, so Brothers is in the queue.

I love crime thrillers and dramas involving family, so Last Seen looks very much like my kind of show. But I haven’t started it yet, despite Stephen King’s endorsement.

Two observations about LAST SEEN, 4 episodes in (Apple+): 1–It's a fantastic show, and 2–I see no good resolution for the families involved. Or for Sarah, who is played beautifully by Chloe Jean Lourdes.

— Stephen King (@StephenKing) September 24, 2026

And these are only the shows currently airing. 

I’m still not caught up on Silo season 3, and haven’t even started Sugar season 2 despite great reviews and being a fan of the show. I could watch more on Apple if I ignored other streamers, but other shows elsewhere are keeping me busy too.

October is right around the corner too, and Apple has a whopping seven new TV shows and movies premiering—the most I can remember in a single month.

All this to say, I’m really pleased that Apple TV is doing so well. It won more Emmys than HBO this year for a reason.

title: Apple adds RAW support for 11 digital cameras across iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Vision Pro
snippet: Apple today updated its official list of digital camera RAW formats supported across its platforms, adding support for 11 models from several manufacturers. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple today updated its official list of digital camera RAW formats supported across its platforms, adding support for 11 models from several manufacturers. Here are the details.

Apple now supports RAW files from 562 cameras

Apple’s operating systems offer system-level support for RAW images captured by many third-party cameras.

In a nutshell, this lets compatible apps work directly with those cameras’ RAW files, allowing them to better adjust elements such as exposure, color, and so on.

That is in contrast with formats such as JPEG, which don’t allow for the same post-processing editing flexibility, since much of that image processing is basically baked into the final image.

Apple maintains support articles listing digital cameras with RAW formats supported by its current (and past) operating systems. The list was updated today, adding 11 digital cameras, bringing the total to 562 models.

title: A Chrome bug is slowing extension load times to a snail’s pace on macOS, Google is aware
snippet: Google Chrome extensions are reportedly taking too long to load on macOS devices, when they should reasonably only take a couple of seconds, due to a bug in the latest updates. Google is aware of the issue. more…
fullText:
Google Chrome extensions are reportedly taking too long to load on macOS devices, when they should reasonably only take a couple of seconds, due to a bug in the latest updates. Google is aware of the issue.

The report comes courtesy of PiunikaWeb, which noted a thread entry on the Chromium issue tracker divulging the issue. The issue seems to affect macOS instances of Google Chrome, rather than Windows or mobile versions. The affected extensions are reportedly taking up to 60 seconds to load, when extensions should open instantly. 

Users began reporting extensions lag in Google Chrome last week, and one of the main third-party tools it seems to affect is password managers like 1Password. The credential management app offers an extremely handy Chrome extension for password autofill across any site that requires you to remember your reasonably complex password. According to the company, it’s aware that a Google Chrome update seems to be slowing extension performance.

Hey Don! There is a known issue in Google Chrome itself right now that can cause extension popups to take much longer than usual to open, and we’d like to figure out if that’s what you’re running into here.

When 1Password is slow or won’t open, do you notice the same thing with…

— 1Password (@1Password) September 16, 2026

It doesn’t seem to only affect 1Password. Some replies indicate other extensions are being affected by the bug, though it doesn’t appear to be consistent.

	

What seems to be causing this disparity in extension load times is mismanaged process priority on Google Chrome’s end, though that hasn’t been verified by Google. Specifically, this seems to happen on macOS 26, and for whatever reason, Google Chrome deems certain extensions a low-priority operation, effectively pushing them to the background while it diverts resources to other tasks. The result is a much longer load time for users.

Google is aware of the issue, posting a reply to the official community page. Here’s what Google’s team says:

We’re continuing to investigate this issue as a priority, and I’ve also asked the team to consider all options including if we can roll the experiment out any further. We’ll make sure to share further updates on this thread as we have them.

Some users have noted that, in the meantime, enabling the PMLoadingPageVoter flag fixes the issue. It’s worth noting that enabling/disabling flags in Google Chrome carries some risk, so please only do so with that in mind.

title: Big Pixel VIPs widget redesign starts rolling out
snippet: Following the version 2.0 update rolling out earlier this week, Google is now beginning to launch the Pixel VIPs widget redesign announced in the September Feature Drop. more…
fullText:
Following the version 2.0 update rolling out earlier this week, Google is now beginning to launch the Pixel VIPs widget redesign announced in the September Feature Drop.

Previously, the widget could be expanded to take up your entire screen. This redesign limits Pixel VIPs to two layouts.

The 5×1 layout shows just one row of your prioritized contacts (up to four) at a time with the ability to scroll for more. This view pairs circular profile avatars with just first names, rather than including surnames as before. The change results in a more consistent widget appearance.

Old vs. new

	

The 5×2 configuration is now the max size for the Pixel VIPs widget. Depending on the number of contacts, Google will display rectangular cards that feature pill-shaped buttons to quickly call or message.

Meanwhile, unread messages will result in a circular badge appearing in the top-right of the circular profile or the messaging icon, which would benefit from being a little bit more noticeable in the latter configuration.

This is rolling out via a server-side update that is not yet widely available. It’s only appearing on one of our Pixel devices today.

Version 2.0 rolled out earlier this week with a fullscreen design that replaces the bottom sheet approach. There are also some tweaks to the feed, while a dock at the bottom of the screen lets you quickly switch between your VIPs.

title: Bellroy’s leather Pixel 11 Pro case is a keeper
snippet: Like any sane capitalist, I love getting new stuff. But there’s something heartening about those new things settling into age, like a fecund garden becoming slightly unwieldy, or a pair of shoes getting more comfortable as you use them. Similarly, I’ve always enjoyed the way a well-made leather case ages as it weathers the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Traditionally called a patina, it’s the lived-in quality that a piece of leather inherits as it absorbs skin oils, scratches, and the unpredictability of weather. more…
fullText:
Like any sane capitalist, I love getting new stuff. But there’s something heartening about those new things settling into age, like a fecund garden becoming slightly unwieldy, or a pair of shoes getting more comfortable as you use them.

Similarly, I’ve always enjoyed the way a well-made leather case ages as it weathers the trials and tribulations of everyday life. Traditionally called a patina, it’s the lived-in quality that a piece of leather inherits as it absorbs skin oils, scratches, and the unpredictability of weather.

So it was when I put on the new “Red Ochre” variant of the leather Pixel 11 Pro XL case from Bellroy. The Melbourne-based company has long been an official Made by Google partner, which means it’s always among the first case manufacturers to unveil its wares each August.

I’ve had the case on my phone for just over three weeks now, and I look forward to picking it up each time. Bellroy’s leather is thin and rigid, and is treated to prevent wear, which means that it takes longer than, say, a piece of Horween leather from Nomad, to age. But it also means it will look new for longer. Barring a few minor scratches, the case has survived more than a few child-related drops with aplomb.

	

On the structure side, the leather is reinforced with a rigid plastic frame that protrudes a millimeter or so above the display, and is covered internally by a microfiber lining. Magnets are present on the back for PixelSnap compatibility, and the buttons are made from anodized aluminum, which gives them a satisfying tactility akin to the phone’s buttons themselves.

At $59, this is not a cheap case, but to my eyes it’s the right combination of form and function. I love the color, though there are three others available — Black, Artichoke, and Pewter — if the more traditional saddle color is a bit too bright.

My weakness is a great leather case for any phone, but unlike iPhone and Galaxy cases there aren’t many good Pixel options. There’s this $40 option made by Snakehive that I plan to pick up, but it lacks coverage on the top, bottom, and right button side, which I dislike. Still, it appears to have more supple leather than Bellroy’s, which should patina more quickly, so I’m looking forward to putting them head-to-head in the future.

Until then, I’m quite happy with Bellroy’s leather Pixel 11 Pro XL case, and plan to keep it on my phone until something else newer, shinier, and patina-ier comes along.

title: Android 17 QPR1 changes some Pixel status bar icons
snippet: This month’s stable release of Android 17 QPR1 comes with some unexpected status bar icon changes on Pixel. more…
fullText:
This month’s stable release of Android 17 QPR1 comes with some unexpected status bar icon changes on Pixel.

The silent or mute icon goes from a crossed-out speaker to a bell.

This might be an accidental regression as Google switched from the bell to the speaker in Android 14. Notably, this change was not present during the Android 17 QPR1 Beta cycle and only went live with the stable OTA this week. 

The speaker icon is still live in 17 QPR2 Beta 5. (Meanwhile, the switcher at the top of the volume slider still uses the bell.)

	

Another icon change further complicates whether this tweak was intentional. The VPN icon is now much thicker and filled in, with this update also only appearing with the stable release.

We’ll know this was a mistake if Google changes it back in future releases, though any fix may not arrive until the sizable QPR2 update in December. Android 17 QPR1 is not yet available for the Pixel 11 series.

title: The Googlebook has an opportunity to build Android like nothing else [Video]
snippet: Despite having effectively zero market share right now, there is an opportunity for Googlebook to do something that basically nobody else could do, but can they do it? more…
fullText:
Despite having effectively zero market share right now, there is an opportunity for Googlebook to do something that basically nobody else could do, but can they do it?

I’ll state right up top that I’m already cautiously optimistic. We need a competitor player to Mac and, in particular, Windows. Microsoft, as of late, has been nothing but combative with the people who use the firm’s operating system every single day. A new player is needed. I’m still not fully convinced yet by Googlebooks, but there is an opportunity, a big opportunity that hinges on quite a few things falling into place.

Considering how many new products are released every year, it’s quite surprising how few operating systems are unveiled. I suppose there is a caveat that Android has existed for a long time, but there have been no true attempts to make it work as a “proper desktop” experience, save Samsung’s DeX system, which was an internal attempt to make it work with Galaxy phones and tablets.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

DeX is a fine take on things, but it is limited by virtue of being an experience trying to emulate a desktop experience. Googlebook OS is Android reimagined for the desktop era.

I’m still not sure if this is too late or if there is enough interest. Google’s move comes at a very interesting time. Maybe its impending launch was the reason that Chrome OS has languished in recent years, having had lots of early promise and a surging user base, particularly in the education sector.

I have had the benefit of trying out Googlebooks, but in the lead-up to launch, I’ve been thinking more broadly about why now, and whether there is any real, tangible reason that Google would fully adopt Android across phones, tablets, and, now, desktops/laptops.

Bear with me, though, as a lot of assumptions have to be made for my points to fully hit home. I know that isn’t ideal, but just indulge me in this thought exercise at the very least.

The high-end might not be the ‘tip of the spear’

We’ve just seen a slew of expensive hardware unveiled under the Googlebook branding. These are the “optimum” hardware experiences, and I do think many are overpriced. That’s not where I see the benefits.

Compared to previous Chrome OS versions, Android devices are better optimized for low-power, low-resource use. A bad Chromebook is almost always worse than a bad Android device, at least in my experience. It’s harder to hide bad performance on a laptop or desktop because you’re used to certain power thresholds. On a tablet or phone, that isn’t as pronounced because things are almost always more lightweight.

It helps that many Android SoCs are powerful enough now to rival mid-range desktop processors or at least those found in notebooks.

Android seems to scale much better now than a few years ago, but as Apple has shown recently, you can run desktop-level applications on mobile SoCs. I could easily see a laptop running absolutely fine with a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 from a few years ago and doing so with very low power consumption.

Just a few years ago, when Google Stadia was still around, the idea of a “gaming Chromebook” felt silly and wasteful. Those machines relied entirely on the cloud, meaning you were paying a premium for a laptop that couldn’t actually play games without perfect Wi-Fi. However, if we get gaming Googlebooks these could be a very different prospect. 

Hardware has evolved to the point where modern mobile processors easily outperform last-generation consoles like the PlayStation 4, bringing entry-level gaming power straight into a laptop chassis without needing an internet connection.

At the same time, the software side has improved drastically. Android gaming is no longer just for casual mobile apps; it now features massive, high-fidelity games that look and feel like console titles. Combined with the ability to emulate older PC and console games locally, a gaming Googlebook becomes a genuine, self-sufficient gaming machine you can actually take anywhere, and one that doesn’t require a wall outlet to play for hours at a time.

Unlike Steam Machines and the Steam Deck, Fortnite is there right from day one.

Something else to consider that I think has been glossed over by basically anyone, because we’re so accustomed to mouse and keyboard interactions with a laptop or desktop.

No other desktop-level operating systems have been developed from the ground up with touch interactions in mind. This is one of the other major USPs for Googlebooks; I’ve already said it multiple times in this rundown that Android only needs to close an application gap. That is exponentially easier than trying to shoehorn a legacy OS into a new form factor.

Apple has kept iOS, iPadOS, and MacOS all as separate OS builds. Google’s “everything is Android” approach could be a masterstroke. I’m resting heavy emphasis on “could” in that equation.

Why? Well, there is a generation of people out there who have grown up effectively “mobile first.” Kids who are now young adults, the “iPad kids” that are now getting to a stage where they are looking for a product that is familiar, comfortable, and does everything they need.

They’ve grown up already using tools like Capcut rather than Adobe. Playing mobile games or mobile ports of the biggest games, like Roblox. Traditional desktop paradigms have never catered to those young people. Googlebooks and the Android experience, rightly or wrongly, extend the familiar to a new form factor. It’s a play that I haven’t seen many discuss, but that could work if the price is right.

‘Desktop-level’ could bring even wider benefits

For the older folks, we have a bee in our bonnets about “desktop-level software”. It’s still essential that we get some things ported over sooner rather than later.

If, for instance, Blackmagic or Adobe port over their respective software packages, Davicini Resolve or Creative Cloud apps to Googlebook, that’s great. 

There’s a hidden secondary benefit, though. The next wave of foldable phones with potential support for desktop apps or desktop app scaling now have access to professional-grade applications in a form factor that is multiple times more portable than a traditional laptop. This extends to tablets, too.

I’m quite bullish that Android tablets could be one of the biggest beneficiaries with the introduction of the Googlebook, that is, if the company is willing to allow more power tools to come to the other versions of Android that the Googlebook OS is based on.

You can rebuke much of what I have said for any number of reasons, but everyone can agree that so much hinges on which brands are willing to start building for Android. Closing this “app gap” is arguably the most important component of the Googlebook during its first year.

I’m cautiously optimistic about the Googlebook program. A fully flexible, malleable operating system that spans regular smartphones, foldables, tablets, laptops, and potentially desktops could do something no other OS has offered before. Scalable in ways that not even Apple has been able to do, but has half-stepped toward since making iPadOS a midway experience or bridge between iOS and Mac.

If Google invests in and enhances Android across the entire stack, every existing and future device will evolve at a rate that wasn’t possible before. Scalable for any screen size. Apps that can be desktop-level while still being mobile native.

There is a big “if” here, and that is the only reason I’m not fully invested yet. The current, glaring software gaps need to be plugged – and plugged fast.

There is a parallel that might prove to be a good omen. Linux has had a massive swell of users over the past year, driven by Valve and, in particular, Steam OS. The success of the Steam Deck has proven that an alternative to Windows can work for gamers.

I’m not sure if we’ll ever get a compatibility layer in Android for various Windows or Linux applications, but who knows. It is not out of the realm of possibility, and if it happens, it’s going to be a major turning point. Google just has to be sure that this is a long-term project, and improving on Chrome OS is a must.

Proton has done wonders for Valve over the past 3 or 4 years. This is a blueprint Google could follow. I do think getting native ports for a few of the biggest applications is all it will take to get more on board. A small swell could quite easily become a bigger wave of app conversion.

A few years ago, if you’d asked me if my gaming PC would ever run an OS other than Windows, I’d have said “never”. I sit here 18 months after ditching it in favor of Linux’s performance gains.

That experience has taught me to be less dismissive of Android on desktop than I was some months ago, and my time playing with the first run of Googlebooks has me excited for what might be coming next for Android.

title: Apple increases interest rate for Apple Card Savings Account
snippet: Good news for Apple Card Savings Account users this morning. Apple and Goldman Sachs have increased the interest rate on the account from 3.4% to 3.5% today. more…
fullText:
Good news for Apple Card Savings Account users this morning. Apple and Goldman Sachs have increased the interest rate on the account from 3.4% to 3.5% today.

title: Meta and YouTube say they will run ads for ‘Musk’ documentary after all
snippet: Two companies now say they will accept advertising for director Alex Gibney’s upcoming documentary about Elon Musk, following earlier reporting that a number of social media platforms had rejected the ads.
fullText:
Two companies now say they will accept advertising for director Alex Gibney’s upcoming documentary about Elon Musk, following earlier reporting that a number of social media platforms had rejected the ads.

The Hollywood Reporter published a story Friday saying that TikTok, Meta, YouTube, and X had all refused to run paid ads promoting the trailer for “Musk.” 

However, when TechCrunch reached out to Meta on Saturday, a spokesperson said, “This was an error and the ads are being restored.” We’ve asked Meta for more details and will update this article if we hear back.

YouTube also posted an update Saturday, noting that “the trailer has always been available on YouTube.” (Indeed, that’s how we were able embed it at the end of this article.) The company added, “When submitted as an ad, it was temporarily restricted by our system. Following review the ad has been cleared to run.”

X’s rejection is unsurprising — Musk, who owns the social media platform, recently posted that “Dogshit is worth more respect than Gibney.” 

But Meta, TikTok, and YouTube reportedly rejected the ad for “political content,” which the platforms have various restrictions on. (Meta said last year that it will stop accepting political ads in the European Union, while TikTok says it doesn’t run them at all.) It’s not clear how a documentary trailer counts as campaign advertising, and the film’s U.S. distributor Bleecker Street told the Hollywood Reporter that it had appealed the rejections.

Gibney has directed acclaimed documentaries including “Going Clear” (about the Church of Scientology) and “The Inventor” (about Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos), as well as a movie about Steve Jobs. “Musk,” his latest, premiered at the Venice International Film Festival earlier this month and has received almost universally positive reviews. The film currently has a 100% “fresh” rating on Rotten Tomatoes and is set for theatrical release in the United States on October 9.

Vulture’s Bilge Ebiri described the nearly four-hour documentary as a revealing look at Musk’s tech career, his alliance with President Donald Trump, and his personal life, with interview subjects including ex-wife Justine Musk and former right-wing influencer Ashley St. Clair (who recently had a child with Musk but now describes him as “a nuke”).

Ebiri wrote that while the film is a “fascinating” character study, adding, “As a tale of modern business, it’s revealing. And as a warning about our future, it’s terrifying.”

Despite the initial wave of critical acclaim, The Hollywood Reporter also said that Universal Pictures was wavering in its commitment to distribute the film internationally, reportedly due to the studio’s fear of angering the Trump administration. (Universal subsequently said it will release the documentary in theaters but is still figuring out its release strategy).

TechCrunch has also reached out to TikTok, X, and Bleecker Street for comment.

This post has been updated to include YouTube’s statement that it has cleared the ad.

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

		

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

You can contact or verify outreach from Anthony by emailing anthony.ha@techcrunch.com.

title: The hottest new hangout for middle schoolers is NPR’s comment section?
snippet: When NPR staffers flagged strange comments under their podcasts on Spotify as bots, it took a Gen Z colleague to (immediately) figure out the mystery.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

1:33 PM PDT · September 25, 2026

Image Credits:Murat Deniz / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Parents have spent years trying to keep their kids off social media, so some kids headed to the one place no adult would think to look for them: NPR.

On this week’s “This American Life,” host Ira Glass tells the story of the team behind NPR’s podcast “Wild Card,” who noticed a flood of baffling comments under their Spotify episodes last fall. A producer assumed the bizarre abbreviations and indecipherable emojis were bot traffic and shared screenshots in NPR’s Slack. They then reported the posts to Spotify.

But Hannah Chin, an audio producer and Gen Z colleague, took a look at the screenshots and recognized, almost immediately by Glass’s telling, that these weren’t bots. They were likely middle schoolers who were too young for social media, running a group chat in the comments of the podcast. (Perhaps someone at NPR should have grokked this sooner: it spotted kids doing the same thing on TED Radio Hour show last year.)

As for why NPR in particular, when Glass tracked down one of the kids to ask, he was given the kind of unvarnished answer that a middle schooler would give: “Um, I think we just, like, looked for podcasts that didn’t have many comments.”

“I tell you, buddy,” responded Glass, who has hosted “This American Life” for three decades, “I do a public radio show, and that hurts a little to hear.”

title: OpenAI accuses Apple of improperly adding new evidence to trade secrets case
snippet: OpenAI and the other defendants in Apple’s trade secret misappropriation lawsuit made a new filing, asking the court to strike two expert declarations and disregard other evidence Apple recently submitted. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
OpenAI and the other defendants in Apple’s trade secret misappropriation lawsuit made a new filing, asking the court to strike two expert declarations and disregard other evidence Apple recently submitted. Here are the details.

A bit of context

As frequent 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple recently filed a trade secret theft lawsuit against OpenAI, Jony Ive’s io Products, and two former employees: Chang Liu and Tang Tan.

In a nutshell, Apple is accusing its former employees of taking or accessing confidential hardware information after leaving the company and using it to benefit OpenAI’s consumer hardware efforts.

Apple has specifically alleged that Chang Liu accessed confidential engineering files after leaving Apple, while alleging that Tang Tan sought confidential information from Apple employees interviewing for jobs.

As part of the lawsuit, Apple has asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction barring OpenAI and the other defendants from accessing, using, disclosing, or soliciting Apple’s confidential information and trade secrets.

According to Apple, the injunction would prevent its trade secrets from becoming further embedded in OpenAI’s hardware development while the case plays out.

Apple files new evidence, OpenAI shoots back

As part of the legal back-and-forth over its motion for this preliminary injunction, Apple last week filed a reply brief supported by five expert declarations totaling 126 pages, along with 13 exhibits. The experts were Daniel Roffman, James Pooley, Dr. Ayman Fayed, Dr. Paul Hatch, and Dr. Jude Runge.

In these documents, Apple argued that OpenAI’s opposition failed to undermine its trade secret claims, and pointed to additional evidence that it says supports its allegations against Liu, Tan, OpenAI, and io Products.

The expert declarations, meanwhile, addressed and further detailed issues such as Apple’s security practices, forensic evidence from Liu’s devices, the value of its power-management trade secrets, and the secrecy of its metal-finishing processes, two key categories at issue in the lawsuit.

Now, OpenAI and the other defendants are shooting back, accusing Apple of improperly using its reply brief to introduce new evidence and expert opinions, including material they say could have been presented earlier, leaving the defendants without a fair opportunity to respond.

From the fling:

Apple submitted with its reply brief five new expert declarations (including one entirely new expert), totaling 126 pages, as well as numerous new exhibits. These declarations go far outside the scope of Apple’s opening brief and Defendants’ opposition, and in any event do not save Apple’s deficient motion.

The defendants also go through the new expert declarations in detail, arguing that Apple is effectively trying to shore up its original motion with new material after seeing the defendants’ response.

Among other things, they argue that Runge was brought in as an entirely new expert to reinforce testimony Apple had already submitted, and that Fayed offered new opinions that could have been included earlier.

They add that Pooley relied on an investigation conducted only after Apple filed its original motion, and that Roffman introduced evidence they say was available to Apple before that filing, while also presenting some of Liu’s communications out of context.

As a result, the defendants are asking the court to strike two of the new declarations, including Roffman’s five exhibits, and disregard other evidence and opinions that they say were improperly introduced.

Interestingly, they ask that if the court decides to consider Roffman’s declaration and exhibits anyway, it also take into account a new declaration Liu filed, offering his own explanation of the messages and device activity that Apple cited as evidence against him.

macOS 27 Golden Gate is a huge upgrade over macOS 26 Tahoe, and not just because of the smarter design decisions. Just like iOS 27 for iPhone, the Mac adds a Liquid Glass appearance slider. This lets you dramatically change the look of your Mac across the system.

The slider

Liquid Glass is Apple’s design language that started with iOS 26 and macOS 26 Tahoe. Initially, Liquid Glass started with a single look. Apple later added a setting to make Liquid Glass less clear.

Starting with iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, Liquid Glass is no longer limited to just two styles. Instead, Apple has introduced an appearance slider. This lets you make Liquid Glass much more clear than before. You can also give Liquid Glass a more opaque look that still looks modern.

macOS 27 Golden Gate defaults to a medium setting. The system also invites you to adjust the slider during initial setup. You can also adjust the slider later in System Settings > Appearance.

The Liquid Glass slider provides a live preview of what to expect from each setting. Three notches suggest most clear, medium, and most opaque. However, you can assign it to any level in between notches as well.

The Dock

The Dock is the most prominent component that changes appearance based on the Liquid Glass slider setting.

It can range from showing your desktop wallpaper in clear definition to being a more opaque and defined material.

Here’s a closer look:

macOS desktop widgets can be full color, dim, or change automatically. The Liquid Glass slider changes how the dim widget appearance looks as well.

Apple Music and Podcasts

Apps like Apple Music and Podcasts that have system Now Playing bars have a very different look based on the Liquid Glass slider position.

Here’s the Now Playing bar Podcasts, for example:

And here’s Music: 

More

The slider also applies to sidebars, toolbars, and toolbar buttons. This changes the look of Photos, Safari, and other apps with window chrome.

The one thing about the Liquid Glass slider in macOS 27 Golden Gate is that a single slider controls all Liquid Glass appearances across the system. That means you get one look for the Dock, widgets, and window chrome. 

What’s your preference? More clear, more opaque, or somewhere in the middle? Personally, I really love how nice and mature the more opaque option looks on my Mac. Still, it can be fun to experiment with more clear, and I’m glad macOS 27 Golden Gate gives everyone the option to decide.

title: Nest Doorbell has been triggering Gemini’s American accent, no matter what language you speak; fix coming
snippet: Google Home is experiencing a unique bug that announces Nest Doorbell notifications in an American accent, even if your preferences are set to literally any other language/dialect. more…
fullText:
Google Home is experiencing a unique bug that announces Nest Doorbell notifications in an American accent, even if your preferences are set to literally any other language/dialect.

According to one user on Reddit, Gemini has been responding to them in American accent only when its referencing their Nest Doorbell. That’s nothing out of the ordinary on the surface, but this user’s complaint revolves entirely around the fact that they’re French, speak French, and live in France. Even still, the Nest Doorbell seems to trigger Gemini’s US English.

It isn’t just affecting one user, or one device. A commenter expressed the same concern in the Netherlands, and another in the UK. For the user in the Netherlands, their Bosch washing machine alerts default to US English instead of Dutch. It sounds like every other interaction with Gemini happens in the language of choice, but certain appliances bring out a different Gemini voice altogether.

According to a response by an official Google account, the issue is being worked on. No fix has been rolled out, but Gemini will likely stop responding in its American accent soon enough, unless you specifically want that.

	

It might have been be a bug developed after the September Google Home update with changes to Gemini for Home. Spoken notifications seem to work as intended, but for whatever reason, Gemini chooses to give the user context in an American accent instead of the language or accent set in preferences. the only change note that refers to Gemini is one that improves follow up question behavior. Beyond that, there’s nothing pointing towards an obvious cause.

Something is clearly broken along the pipeline of information, but it’s manifesting in one of the most hilarious ways.

It’s a strange one, but Google is aware of the issue and claims to be working on it.

title: Apple retires the Apple Park Visitor Center’s unique AR experience
snippet: Earlier this summer, Apple closed a portion of the Apple Park Visitor Center as it worked to “improve our store.” That space has now reopened, and the big change is that Apple has removed the augmented reality experience that let visitors use custom iPads to view Apple Park. more…
fullText:
Earlier this summer, Apple closed a portion of the Apple Park Visitor Center as it worked to “improve our store.”

That space has now reopened, and the big change is that Apple has removed the augmented reality experience that let visitors use custom iPads to view Apple Park.

When Apple opened the Apple Park Visitor Center to the public in 2017, here’s how the company touted the AR experience:

Inviting guests to explore Apple Park in an immersive and engaging way, a 3-D model of the campus is brought to life by augmented reality technology.

Visitors can learn about the world’s largest naturally ventilated building and view one of the largest on-site solar energy installations in the world. Visitors can also choose to lift the entire roof off the building to peek inside to the collaborative office pod layout.

Until this change, the Apple Park Visitor was divided into three sections: the AR exhibit, a traditional-style Apple Store, and a cafe.

Source: RedNote

Now, Apple has retired the AR exhibit and transformed that space into an extension of the more traditional Apple Store. As spotted by MacRumors, this includes Avenues along the wall showcasing accessories and redesigned display tables featuring Apple products.

The rest of the Apple Park Visitor Center, including the cafe, remains unchanged.

9to5Mac’s Take

The AR experience at the Apple Park Visitor Center was unique, but after nine years it was starting to feel like that space could be better utilized in other ways. 

I wish Apple had tried something other than converting it into a traditional retail store, but at least the cafe remains as a unique fixture of the Apple Park Visitor Center.

title: Apple Photos in iOS 27 gets camera roll feature it’s long needed
snippet: iOS 27 is a big update for Apple’s Photos app, with improvements to slideshows, shared albums, and more. It also adds a welcome camera roll-type feature many have long been asking for: ‘Captured by Me.’ more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is a big update for Apple’s Photos app, with improvements to slideshows, shared albums, and more. It also adds a welcome camera roll-type feature many have long been asking for: ‘Captured by Me.’

‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 Photos app contains only photos and videos you shot in Camera app

Apple’s Photos app has steadily expanded its feature set over the years. In addition to being home to the photos and videos your iPhone captures, it also includes content that’s been shared with you, Memories, screenshots, saved media, and a lot more.

The Photos app used to offer a ‘Camera Roll’ feature that was similar to what the ‘Recents’ album does today. It included images you captured as well as ones you saved.

But what’s been missing for a long time is a feature that actually just shows photos and videos that you’ve taken—in other words, something that could more accurately be called your ‘camera roll.’

iOS 27 delivers that long-missing feature, and it’s called ‘Captured by Me.’

‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 is a new Photos collection that does exactly what it sounds like. It includes only media that’s been captured by your Camera app.

So photos and videos that you shot on your iPhone are collected there. But you won’t see screenshots, images your friends sent you, or any other types of content.

In addition to the dedicated ‘Captured by Me’ collection, you can also use a ‘Captured by Me’ filter in your main Photos library.

Whichever way you use the feature, ‘Captured by Me’ in iOS 27 fills an important gap in Apple Photos’ feature set.

title: What I learned after 30 days with the Pixel 11 [Video]
snippet: It has been almost 30 days since Google officially launched the Pixel 11 lineup, and the 11 might be the most sensible device of the bunch. Here’s what I have learned, having used it for the full month post-launch. more…
fullText:
It has been almost 30 days since Google officially launched the Pixel 11 lineup, and the 11 might be the most sensible device of the bunch. Here’s what I have learned, having used it for the full month post-launch.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Less nip, more tuck

It’s hard to be annoyed too much about the Pixel 11 design, but I can 100% get a little bored. When you get a new phone, you may subconsciously want at least a few changes to help it feel “different.”

However, if you’ve not used the Pixel 9 or Pixel 10, you probably won’t even care. I know I’m not in the minority in loving the Pixel design, but there’s certainly a feeling of Groundhog Day after a while. What I’ve realized is that, as someone who has used the last three generations, to me, a case has felt more important than ever.

	

After a month of use, the flatter camera visor is one of the few “big” changes that feels more consequential. My dream would be a boxier shape akin to the Pixel 10a, but with a case on the phone, you can achieve that, or close to it.

A tangible change I hadn’t expected was the NFC chip moving closer to the top edge. In tandem with the smaller camera protrusion, I’m not clashing my phone against terminals or turnstiles, plus wireless payments are a lot faster, or at least feel more accurate.

I’m so glad we have stronger Pixelsnap magnets because you’re confident an accessory will stick, which is especially important because the slippery, glossy finish on the back glass was problematic with the Pixel 10 at times. I do wish that the phone didn’t sound so hollow to the tap, for a $900 phone, it can feel a little cheap, even though it has a great frame and mass. Little nitpicks, but I do care about extra attention in these areas. Maybe next year it’s time to address these admittedly minor build complaints.

As far as the design is concerned, the Pixel 11 builds on what was good; the good news is that there is very little bad. I hoped that we would get display brightness changes, but maybe it’s the endgame for this specific size and shape. I’m very unsure how Google will make major changes next year if we do get a proposed redesign. The only way I can see changes is in the materials used, some dimension shavings, but little else that can really refine the post-Pixel 9 formula. 

Does Gemini Intelligence matter?

I mean this in the most positive way possible. The Pixel 11 is more of the same, yet there are a few things that start to feel like they haven’t become game-changing in the ways that Google seems to expect. I’m not actively using many of the new functions that the Pixel 11 shipped with. I say “actively” as the hands-off background automation approach is what Google should excel at and isn’t quite doing so everywhere yet.

Proactive Assistance is on the cusp of being a truly exceptional upgrade for Magic Cue. I’m in the UK, so Google Messages is an app that I love, but don’t use with many contacts. I say this because when I’ve had suggestions for things like my passport number or my flight number on a trip, the instantaneous pop-up suggestions seem so perfectly integrated that it feels like Magic Cue on steroids.

We desperately need to get this into third-party applications as soon as possible. It would save me so much time and effort in WhatsApp chats that I’m sort of frustrated it isn’t system-wide yet.

Now that I’ve been using Rambler for an extended period, I’ve made a U-turn on its inclusion, and I’m trusting it more to take notes, send long messages, and dare I say it, compose a few important emails…It’s a sleeper function that I’m enjoying greatly as a lazy typer. I even drafted a few paragraphs of this extended review using Rambler. Add in live transcripts, and it’ll become a “must have” for the lazy among us.

I completely forgot that Pause Point was already on Pixel 11. I’ve tried it a few times, and I don’t know why it isn’t being touted as a bigger deal. It’s one of the few Digital Wellbeing tools that feels like it could curb your phone usage. The rest of the AI stack? It all still feels a little filler. I’m still using Pixel Screenshots on an almost daily basis, but I’m still not finding ways to use many of the major functions that Google keeps touting because of the aforementioned first-party app requirements.

I mentioned modem issues in my initial review; these were temporary. Fully resolved, there is no doubt in my mind that the modem handles signal way better than the Pixel 9 and 10, and VPN connection woes are gone with the last couple of OTA updates, too.

Finally, a quality camera…again

I’m so glad that Google paid attention to some of the major complaints with the Pixel 10 and put in a “proper” big main sensor rather than short-changing buyers with an A-series sensor. The quality jump just gives me confidence that you’re properly equipped for every eventuality.

Next year, I’m fully hoping for some improved ultrawide and telephoto hardware.

To the surprise of nobody, Camera Looks is my outright most used function across every facet of the Pixel 11 this year so far. In the back of my mind, with just about any Pixel, having consistency has been both a blessing and a curse. I spoke about this last year when switching away to Zerocam on the Pixel 10 Pro. I wanted less processing done on my behalf, and Camera Looks just answers that with aplomb.

I have completely switched to using the “Shadows” look. It’s my default setting, and like when using Zerocam, I’m being more picky about what photos I’m taking with this phone. My only gripe is that the recipes you can cook up would be great if saved for specific circumstances. Being able to save these as custom looks with unique names would be a godsend and a real timesaver.

If you just want pure consistency, stick with the default settings and enjoy another great camera with better zoom, a quality main sensor; the rest is just more of the same – which is to say very good for this price bracket.

I wish I had more reasons to use Magic Camera, as my colleague Daniel Bader so aptly states, this is the ultimate family camera function. The outputs are great, and getting both video and photo at the same time is perfect, as you preserve the moment no matter what. 

As I say, maybe I need to force myself to use it more often. I’ve barely touched it since my first week of testing, but I’m more at home playing with regular photos and don’t often need snapshots from Magic Camera. There are people who are going to use this practically every day. I am not one of those people.

Loving the longevity

I can’t say I’ve had a problem with a recent Pixel phone, but the 11 is really solid. I’ve been on a few weekend trips already with this phone, and it hasn’t let me down. Side note: I actually like the AI summaries for battery usage. It feels better tailored than just the list of apps. It’s fairly recent, but I like this tweak and hope it improves over time.

There’s only so many times I can complain about the charging speed before you sort of come to terms with it. At least the Qi2 charging speed has increased to 25W, which isn’t a million miles away from the wired charging speed now. Just give us a little more, and I’ll be happier. That said, I started charging overnight again quite recently, so my complaint is a little moot.

For what it’s worth, the Pixel 11 lasts longer than my Pixel 11 Pro, which is solid and dependable. It’s been a long time since a Pixel had a terrible battery lifespan, put it that way.

What’s it like to own the Pixel 11, and is it worth it?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

2026 feels like a sobering year for technology. Not only has real progress slowed drastically in the areas outside artificial intelligence, but we’re expected to pay more for the privilege.

There is a good phone underneath the price hikes. One that, yes, hasn’t changed all that much.

Luckily for most people, the Pixel 11 isn’t as compromised as the Pro models. For a long time, I felt that this was where Google did the best work outside of the A-series. A solid base for all the functionality and features a “normie” would and could want from their mobile companion.

Because the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL have some cost prohibitive compromizes, there’s a cost incentive to go for the base model once again. I still struggle to fully recommend that anyone buy the Pixel 11, but it’s the most sensible of the bunch.

We’ll revisit the Pixel 11 again in the next few months to determine what has held up and what hasn’t, so if you prefer even longer testing periods, then check back in another 60-ish days for an updated verdict.
